BasePK: 3540384

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the Government is totally without shame. It has misled the senior citizens of the country. Like the rest of Canadians who were promised all sorts of goodies during the election campaign, the senior citizens saw the Tory Government do an about face following its election. One of its members even had the nerve to say that the Government is not committed in any way to respecting the promises that were made.
It is unacceptable, Mr. Speaker, for two Tory losers like Roy McMurtry and Lawrence Hanigan to be appointed to fat cat government jobs and have their salaries increased by almost $60,000 per year, while senior citizens of my riding will each be losing $100 this year. The salary increase for those two Tory appointees is enough to restore the full indexation of OAS to every one of the 6,000 senior citizens in my riding.
I urge the Government to cancel the salary increases of these two Tories, and to restore immediately those benefits to the senior citizens of my riding. I am sure there is enough money wasted by the Government in every other riding of the country to restore full benefits to everyone.
* [DOT] *

For each speech, return valid JSON with two fields:

BasePK: 3540417

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I think the elderly in Canada would be more inclined to believe in the Hon. Member's sincerity if, as a member of a Liberal Government, he had not been involved in severely cutting back benefits for the elderly in 1982. And since the Hon. Member, who was a Minister at the time, took that kind of action, it is clear his credibility has suffered as a result. The provision has had no negative impact on the elderly. According to the Budget, this measure would and will become effective on January 1 of next year, but also according to the Budget, we are monitoring the situation on a regular basis to ensure, as far as possible, that no problems will result for the neediest in our society.

BasePK: 3540481

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Pensioners across the country fully understand that the budgetary proposal will not come into effect until January 1 of next year, and that is precisely

June 14, 1985
Oral Questions
why they are now organizing. Senior citizens have sharpened their pencils and they know very well, because of the way they have to live, what the impact of this proposal will be.
If the Prime Minister is seriously concerned about how pensioners feel, I suggest to him that there is no need to monitor the situation between now and the end of this year, because the effects of the proposal will not be felt until 1986. I would ask the Prime Minister if he will not say to the pensioners that he promised them during the election campaign, and following that, that he would not touch Old Age Security benefits, and that he will rise in his place today to fulfil that commitment.

BasePK: 3540512

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue which is about another, admittedly smaller, haemorrhage of public funds. Yesterday the Minister of National Revenue refused to answer the question about the very strange decision of National Revenue in its treatment of the bank account of Crosbie Offshore Services Limited. He indicated that Section 241 of the Income Tax Act prevented him from answering the question. That Section is there to protect the confidentiality of the taxpayer. I would remind the Minister, in this case, that the taxpayer waived that confidentiality by making information public. The Minister of Justice has also made the information public about that tax account, so I feel justified in asking him again why this very strange behaviour. Why, when Revenue Canada could have paid itself that debt, did it release the funds, and it now stands at least $332,000 short, possibly more?

June 14, 1985
Oral Questions

BasePK: 3540529

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Last March his Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion said that while discussions continued for a new agreement with Japan on the export of Japanese cars to Canada, the situation would be monitored to ensure that the provisions of the previous agreement would be respected. Yet in April exports of Japanese cars to Canada jumped 20 per cent, and 27 per cent in May. Yesterday his Minister told the press that he was dropping the requirement of the previous agreement that the total number of Japanese cars exported to Canada not exceed 170,000.
1 ask the Prime Minister why his Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion has not carried out his commitment to see that the previous agreement was respected, and why has he dropped the key provision of that agreement without getting anything in return by way of either a new agreement at previous levels, or new commitments on Canadian content, jobs, and production for Canada.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, 1 also have a question for the Right Hon. Prime Minister.
First of all, I would like to say that as far as I am concerned, he is certainly to be commended for indicating in the Budget that the situation with respect to Old Age Security pensions will be reviewed.
He deserves to be congratulated on having said that he is going to monitor the situation between now and the end of the year, and that he is disposed to make changes if necessary.

June 14, 1985
Committee Reports
However, what I fail to understand, and that is the point of my question, is why this potential cut in the level of indexation was put in the Budget? Why was it included? The monitoring could have been done until the end of this year without causing any anxiety among the elderly, or as they say in Quebec: "sans jouer avec leurs nerfs". And the decision could have been made at the end of this year just the same. Why did the Government decide to have this sword of Damocles hanging over the elderly? Why did they not-

BasePK: 3540553

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's comments. I think he puts the problem in a practical perspective that shows he likes to take a more realistic view.
All the budgetary measures were designed with a view towards setting up stronger social programs at the national level that can be guaranteed to benefit the neediest in our society. That was the whole point of putting our public finances on a sounder basis, after they had been seriously undermined in the past.
When 30, 40 or 50 per cent of the Government of Canada's national assets is spent on paying the interest on the public debt, it is a serious threat to the social programs we want to protect, and that is why we have proceeded in this way.
However, 1 admit the Hon. Member has a point, and that is why we said in the Budget that we were going to monitor the situation very closely in order to try and help the elderly as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my good friend for another splendid question. What one can derive in the way of lessons from the experience of the late 1940s would suggest one particular word of wisdom for the Government in its present circumstances. I am saying that against the background which my friend has evoked of the summit of the Prime Minister with the President of the United States in which it was suggested that all sorts of good things will follow from the fine relations between the two countries. What Canadians so often forget-and I trust the Prime Minister knows better-is that the American constitution provides for a division of power in which the President has limited authority on many of these matters. He certainly faces the actions of a Congress made up of hundreds of Members representing their districts from coast to coast, and two Senators from every state, all of whom will go their own way. The President might conceivably have the best of intentions, but if those Congressmen do not agree with the decisions he has arrived at, he will not get anywhere.
I think of the late 1940s. The key point in the circumstances of 1947 through 1949 was that the dealings from executive to executive were not nearly as effective by themselves as the Government's holding out the prospect, or the fear, to the American administration and to Congress that the Canadian response in the way of trade restraints, which would be made necessary by our shortage of American dollars at the time, would have a very serious effect in one area or another of the United States. In each of those areas where a congressional
Borrowing Authority Act
district was involved there was a Congressman who was going to feel the direct impact of Canadian action.
The moral of the story is that a Government which can only see Americans as friends, instead of realizing the need to be businesslike and tough at times with them, will lose the opportunity to drive home to Americans that if they set out to hurt us, as happens in area after area, we may have to take action to hurt them in Michigan and other parts of the United States. I have yet to see that kind of toughness from this Government.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) raised a very important matter. I appreciate his question. He drew some similarities between the problems of fishermen in Atlantic Canada and the problems of farmers. Clearly there are some comparisons which can be made.
I should like to look at the quotas and countervail duties which have been imposed by the United States. In fact, last week it imposed a duty on fish from Atlantic Canada of approximately 20 per cent, while at the same time it imposed a countervail duty on our hogs of some 5.5 cents per pound. This is having a devastating impact on the price of hogs and has had such an impact since April 1 when the United States imposed it. We certainly see the similarity. There is sort of similarity in the approach of the United States, despite the comments of the Prime Minister about how he will improve trade relations.

June 17, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
1 cannot remember, in the 17 years I have been a Member of Parliament, so many duties, countervails and threats of countervails being imposed. They are all on our primary producers who are already faced with very low commodity prices, for example, fish, agricultural products and softwood lumber. I do not believe anyone in the House will remember such massive countervails and quota plans between Canada and the United States in the past. It is clear that the Government is messing up our entire relationship in terms of those products, all of which have been in very low price positions for the last while.
With regard to the Hon. Member's question concerning duplication of federal and provincial government programs, I doubt that there is that much duplication. For instance, if we look at crop insurance, the federal Government has put up half the premiums and the producers have put up the other half. In most cases the provincial Governments have administered the crop insurance program. It has been a very beneficial program. The Minister runs around the country proclaiming what he has done for farmers since last September 4. One figure he quotes is something like $530 million which has been paid out in crop insurance. That is an insurance program which the former Liberal Government put in place, into which producers pay. As well, the federal Government pays into a fund and the provincial Governments administer the program at a relatively small cost compared with the cost of the premiums for the program. If the Government is proposing that provincial Governments, as I understand it is doing, will put up a third of the cost, similar to the proposed tripartite red meat stabilization program, I think it will find a very cool reception. The reception on the part of provincial Governments having to put up as much as the federal Government will be about as cool as the reception of the deindexation of old age pensions on the part of Atlantic Premiers, all of whom are Conservatives. I do not think many provincial Governments are prepared to put up that additional money for the crop insurance program.
With regard to research and so on, it seems to me that the money spent on research and on developing new varieties of grain, fruit and vegetables, is really a reach toward the future. If we develop a grain which is more hardy or more resistant to disease or will produce greater yields by 5 per cent or 10 per cent, that is the price we pay to be successful five, ten or fifteen years down the road.
In the tripartite red meat stabilization hearings, we heard that provincial Governments in the Maritime Provinces really wanted to see feed freight assistance provided, whether it was provided through the stabilization program or through a direct feed freight assistance program. I do not think they want to see the Government cutting back on it. It seems to me that the Government should be providing a feed freight assistance program, while at the same time doing the necessary research and development to make Atlantic Canada self-sufficient in grain so that hog and beef production can continue there, even though in the initial drafting of the tripartite red meat stabilization program they may not be qualified.
So I think the Hon. Member has raised some very important points concerning the Government's attitude towards management, where it essentially wants to cut back on programs like agricultural assistance, feed freight assistance, grain inspection and crop insurance.

However, we do use a Bill such as C-51 to question the Government's wisdom in spending that borrowed money. From time to time we put forward suggestions as to how we on this side of the House think the money should be spent. For example, in my opinion very often public funds are spent frivolously by this Government, and this is true of other Governments in the past.

It is not a symbol of office, it is an emblem of Canada. If any person in this country should have the right to use that emblem, it is not the Prime Minister, it is the Governor General. Mr. Speaker, I have had an opportunity both at second reading and in committee to make my representations with respect to this Bill. I believe that this Bill has the unanimous support of the House in terms of its content. There is one amendment on which I will say a few words and repeat an undertaking that I believe the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) brought to the attention of the House, both at second reading and at committee, which resulted in a change to the Bill. I would like to also make one or two comments prior to doing that.
I think it is very important to understand that the purpose of this Bill is not to change policy. This Bill was brought in because lawyers in the Department of Justice thought that more than 55 Acts of Parliament as they stood would be viewed by courts as unconstitutional. As a result of that there were changes that were made, some of the changes being very significant.
In my view, and this is a personal impression, the powers with respect to search and seizure were long overdue, were absolutely necessary and as a result of a case that went to the Ontario Court of Appeal, the Southam case, we found that dramatically changed the search and seizure provisions which I think inure to the protection of individual rights. I certainly applaud this change in so many statutes. We even see statutes now with respect to the Income Tax Act where the powers of search and seizure have been dramatically circumscribed.
With respect to the question of the Immigration Act, which was the subject matter of the only amendment in the immigration Act, the Act as it read previously, Section 29(2) and Section 29(3) said this:
(2)	At the request or with the permission of the person with respect to whom an inquiry is to be held, an adjudicator shall allow any person to attend an inquiry if such attendance is not likely to impede the inquiry.
(3)	Except as provided in subsection (2), an inquiry by an adjudicator shall be held in camera.
There was no practical criticism with respect to the handling of this particular procedure prior to this Bill. The Hon. Member for Spadina brought up the point that as a result of the prospective amendment, which was Section 112, of the new Bill that what might happen with respect to this matter is that there could be circumstances under which a refugee might not

June 20, 1985
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms want to disclose publicly to some people who might be in attendance or to some newspaper reporters who might be there the circumstances under which he was claiming the status of refugee for fear that certain consequences might ensue. This might very well be not only to him, but to members of his family. It might be people behind the Iron Curtain, it might be people in Chile, it might be people in many other countries where the public circumstances would be of such a nature that great harm could occur to the family.
This is something that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cros-bie), myself and all members of the Committee thought was a legitimate criticism and which prompted an amendment which I thought was satisfactory and which was agreed upon. That amendment is as follows: Section 112(3) now reads as a result of the amendment, Mr. Speaker, "except as provided in Subsection (2), an inquiry by an adjudicator shall be held in camera unless it is established to the satisfaction of the adjudicator on application by a member of the public that the conduct of the inquiry in public would not impede the inquiry and that the person with respect to whom the inquiry is to be held or any member of that person's family would not be adversely affected if the inquiry were to be held or conducted in public".
In addition to this particular amendment, there was an undertaking that representatives for the Department of Immigration and Employment and the Minister would closely monitor the actual workings of this amendment to ensure that no harm occurred in circumstances where potential refugees were making application for that status.
The Bill as a whole, and I have said this before, is a grat improvement because it puts in constitutional order many federal statutes that, with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, might very well be held to be unconstitutional. It is no panacea. It is not the end of the process. Many Bills come before Parliament now that the Charter is here, where the Charter provisions have to be taken into consideration in terms of the due process. It is a start. It is a very, very substantial move forward. It is not the end of the line.
I hope that all Members of all Parties will believe that this is progress.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak for a moment on my amendment. During the course of this Bill, we heard representation from right across the country and there was some disturbing testimony, to my mind.
June 26, 1985

As you will know, Mr. Speaker, from having read the Bill and being thoroughly acquainted with it, this Bill is permissive legislation which sets out an umbrella under which producers, the provincial Governments and the federal Government can go together to strike a tripartite agreement to stabilize farm prices.
One thing that we heard most often from provinces across the country was that they were concerned about going into these agreements without having some feeling of acceptance or right to raise the possibility of variations in production costs from one end of the country to the other. They felt that there should be some way that would enable them to bring to the discussions the question of the particular costs that they have that are particular to their region, to put those on the table and negotiate the kind of system that is needed for a tripartite system across the country.
Because this is a government Bill, and the motivation is here and the expenditure plans that limit what a private member or an opposition Member can do, this is one of the few places where it is possible to bring the question of regional costs into the discussions. It would be under the section of the activities of the board that was established to look at the costing formula, either for those products that come under the program under the old Agricultural Stabilization Act or products which would come under by tripartite agreements between the various producer groups in the country, some or all of the provinces and the federal Government. This is one of the few spots where it is possible to mention the fact that regional costs can be a concern.
This would put a discussion of these various costs onto the table and permit the various groups to discuss costs that are unique to their parts of the country. For instance, there are high energy costs paid by Prince Edward Island farmers who produce hogs or dairy products. These farmers are required to spend a great deal of money on electricity to run the machinery and sometimes even to provide additional heat.
Representatives from other regions of the country mentioned that feed costs were relatively higher in their regions than in other parts of the country, and they said that they would like to be able to discuss this in the negotiations that take place prior to agreeing to a tripartite system. In fact, they mentioned that they would even like to be able to permit some slight variation with agreement from all of the participating groups as part of the final agreement.
In committee, we heard from representatives of the Province of British Columbia, a province which has had the most experience with an income stabilization program. Those representatives told us that when that program began, there was some allowance for regional differences in costs from one valley to another for the various payout levels in the production of tomatoes and other such crops. However, the representatives went on to point out that as time went on, it became obvious even to the producers that some of these cost disadvantages were offset by advantages in other portions of production
Agricultural Stabilization Act
costs and that eventually regional cost variations were seen to be unnecessary. Therefore, the producers themselves took regional cost variations out of the program.
It is my contention that once producers can see all of the various cost items that producers from their areas and other areas have to face, they will see that there is a real reason for their particular product being produced in their particular corner of the country. There is no doubt that hogs will continue to be produced in Prince Edward Island, Quebec and right across to British Columbia whether or not there is a tripartite stabilization program. While Quebec may have some disadvantages in the area of feed costs, it has an advantage over other parts of the country in labour costs, in the technical programs that are in place and because of the fact that its production units are somewhat superior to those in other parts of the country. That would balance off against the relatively lower cost of grain in Saskatchewan where the production units may not as a general rule be quite up to the competitive standards of those in Quebec.
I maintain that it all evens out. What I am fearful of in permitting this Bill to go through the way it is written without some recognition of regional cost variations is that we will leave the impression on those groups that think they have a particular cost disadvantage that there is no point in coming forward to the bargaining table to participate in the process. The idea behind this particular amendment is to make the umbrella slightly larger so that more producer groups from more provinces will feel comfortable under that umbrella and will begin the discussions preliminary to the establishment of a tripartite program. I think that this amendment sends the message that all producer groups from all across Canada are welcome under that umbrella and that their particular viewpoints and problems will be discussed fully. It will not leave them with the impression that we are excluding some groups while accepting others. That is why I have moved this amendment to the Bill.

On January 24, 1985, Mr. Brian O'Regan, Vice-President of public affairs at Northern Telecom, requested that Canada undertake an official mission to support Northern Telecom's efforts in securing a $487 million contract with the Algerian Government, representing 7,000 person years of employment for Canadians over a five-year period. This request was supported by officials in both the Department of Communications and External Affairs and was then recommended to the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse).
The main thrust of this official mission was to support the bid of Northern Telecom. In view of the considerable Canadian business interests in various industries currently under way in northern Africa and the Middle East, it was deemed opportune and useful for the Minister to take advantage of the request from Northern Telecom to show the Government of Canada's support for these additional business endeavors.
These companies included Radio Canada International; Bell Canada International, as well as other Canadian companies with $400 million in projects completed to date in addition to $1 billion in potential contracts.
With the preliminary planning for a visit to Algeria under way, External Affairs requested through the international relations branch in the Department of Communications that the Minister officiate at the opening of the new Canadian embassy complex in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. In addition to this request, Department of Communications officials informed the Minister that a Montreal-based company was pursuing a major spectrum management contract with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. As the responsibility for this contract was in the control of Dr. Kayal, Minister of Post, Telephone and Telecommunications for the kingdom, a meeting was requested between the two Ministers to discuss the contract as well as to renew co-operation between Canada and Saudi Arabia.
As is normal practice, commercial flights for this trip were investigated but, given the commitment of the Minister for April 9 to address the conference of the Canadian Cable and Television Association in Toronto, the requirement for his attendance at the meeting of the Priorities and Planning Committee on April 16, 1985, as well as the religious holidays one must observe when in Moslem countries, the commercial option was impossible.
To demonstrate the logistical problems experienced in travelling to Algeria, it should be noted that the two ministerial assistants, who accompanied the Minister during his visit in the Middle East, travelled to Paris commercially where they experienced a 36-hour delay before available seating on a connecting flight to Algiers could be confirmed.
The Hon. Member also made a number of substantially incorrect statements in a radio interview in April. First, the Minister's trip did not take him to Israel as alleged by the Hon. Member. The stop-over in Greece was a mandatory refuelling stop and maintenance operation in accordance with Department of Transport regulations. It was not a stop requested by the Minister or any of the passengers.
1 hope, Mr. Speaker, that this information answers some of the concerns of the Hon. Member. I will be happy to answer any further questions he wishes to place to me at a later date.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time concerning a question I directed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on May 24, 1985 regarding the announced closure of the Cape Breton heavy water plants in Glace Bay and in Port Hawkesbury, Nova Scotia.
At that time I indicated to the House, and in particular to the Minister of Finance, that certain assurances were given to the workers of those two plants prior to the particular announcement which was made in the Budget. Again I want to quote, for Your Honour's edification, as I am sure you are concerned about the workers and their families in my riding and in the Port Hawkesbury area, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) who indicated on a couple of occasions that there would be no closure of those plants until alternate employment took place. Since the closure of the two heavy water plants there have been no new jobs for those workers, absolutely none. There has been an agreement by the union representing the employees and by management representatives in regard to a severance package. That particular severance package goes beyond the collective agreement. It is certainly not a rich package, by any means; it is not rich at all. It fails to address a number of important measures. However, in view of the position of the union, which has attempted to represent those workers to the best of its ability, that was all that management and the Government was prepared to do for those employees. The bigger issue is alternate employment.
The Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) gave the impression to many media members that something great and specific would be done forthwith. All

that has been done by the Conservative Government in Ottawa and by the Conservative Government in Nova Scotia has been merely in the area of media news releases. Nothing concrete or specific has been done for that area of Canada by the Tory provincial Government or the Tory federal Government. There are things which they could have done and still could to in terms of relocating and allocating moneys, perhaps for automotive companies, whether it be Hyundai or other foreign manufacturers. There is no concern for the workers in that region of the country. It is the same old story-the theory of trickle down economics practised by the Conservative Government in Ottawa. The thrust of the thesis is very clear, that hopefully at some point in time when the wealthier regions of the country create even more wealth and more jobs, somehow, by some miracle, it will seep down into the less fortunate areas.
My Party and I believe that there is a major national role to be played by the national Government. Mr. Speaker, why is there one set of rules when the Government makes a mistake respecting rich people and another when it makes a mistake affecting ordinary Canadians? The Government made a mistake-a very high level mistake-when it took part in an attempt to rescue the Canadian Commercial Bank. As a result, depositors thought that the bank was basically sound. Now that the bank has failed in spite of the Government's assurances, the Government plans to make good its mistake and to use taxpayers' money to bail out depositors. That is how the Government acts when it makes a mistake which affects the well-to-do, but what happens when a Government mistake affects ordinary Canadians?
Between 1982 and 1984 the Government miscalculated and overpaid rent subsidies for married quarters at CFB Esquimalt. Now that this $.5 million mistake has been discovered by the auditors, the Government is deducting the overpayment from the pay cheques of those people who are still in the services. Individual debts range from $100 to $1,700. At the very time when rent increases will strain family budgets, service people face the additional burden of paying for a government mistake. Why can we not have justice rather than a double standard?

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my Party I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-64, which proposes amendments, in part, to the Seeds Act. We know that while the Bill is an important one it is really a housekeeping Bill and one which wil not raise a major controversy in the House today. Since the Minister is here today in the House, I am sure he will undoubtedly use the opportunity to announce other interesting and productive measures for the agricultural industry of Canada. September 25, 1985
Statements by Ministers
in the course of our history, have suffered from discrimination. It was perfectly clear to any prudent banker that these individuals had carried on imprudent banking practices, but the Minister of State for Finance said that that was good enough for her, that she had full faith in these characters. Mr. Speaker, that is why we, as responsible parliamentarians, plead for an opportunity to do the job that we were elected to do, that is to ensure that every dollar of taxpayers' money is wisely spent. September 26, 1985

There is no country more vulnerable to exchange movement in the American dollar than Canada. Billions of dollars cross our border every day. We have a mutual trade of $150 billion. Yet we were not informed of this. We are now entering a free trade negotiation with the United States while our potential partner did not have the decency or foresight to inform its future partner of an exchange rate movement, something which is frankly more important than the tariff levels to which I will turn in a moment. If that is the type of special relationship the Prime Minister now has with the President of the United States, it is certainly not the kind of special relationship that bears up in a matter of substance.
Tariff barriers have been reduced gradually and progressively throughout the negotiations on the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. By 1987, 80 per cent of our trade with the United States will be free of tariffs and 15 per cent of our trade will be subject to tariffs of 5 per cent or less. That means that 95 per cent of all Canadian goods moving across the American border is already subject to a maximum tariff of 5 per cent or is not subject to a tariff at all. Movements in the exchange rate are now more important than or equally as important as the remaining tariffs. It is the non-tariff barriers about which we must worry.
The key area for discussion and negotiation continues to be non-tariff barriers like subsidies, regulations and procurement policies. The non-tariff barriers in the United States are protected under a new guise. It is a political, economic and legal one. It can be harassment of all three kinds with the way the United States economy operates. We have to know the impact of these negotiations regarding non-tariff barriers on the various regions and sectors of Canada.
In order to eliminate those non-tariff barriers, procurement policies of the provinces and of the states and exports subsidies, only a new style of treaty will work. What will work is not an agreement but a treaty binding the federal and state Governments of the United States and the federal and provincial Governments of Canada. We should not allow pressure from the United States Government to force us to include certain items as non-tariff barriers in the discussions.
Washington has a new vocabulary. The people there like to call negotiations on trade negotiations for a level playing field. A level playing field is local vocabulary for a preoccupation with hidden and overt subsidies that foreign governments provide for exports. Americans and the Congress in particular equate subsidies to so-called unfair competition. There are a whole range of subsidies now subject to countervailing duties. Among those subsidies are subsidies that go right to the heart of the regional economic development policy of this country.
We want a full declaration from the Government indicating how it intends to treat the following items in its negotiations with the United States: social programs, health care, unemployment insurance, which has already been considered a subsidy by some in the United States, family allowances and pensions. What are we going to do about the independence and integrity of our cultural industries? What about the independence, strength and ownership of our financial industries?
Statements by Ministers
What about agricultural support? What about the Canadian Wheat Board? What about all the marketing boards? What about the initial payment under the Wheat Board, something which has been considered by the United States to be a hidden subsidy? What about the auto pact?
We take the view that the auto pact ought not to be included in these negotiations. We take the view that a special arrangement ought to be made for agriculture and that our cultural and financial industries should remain intact.
What about equalization payments? Those could be considered hidden subsidies open to countervail unless they are specifically included in an agreement. What about export incentives for industries in the provinces that have sales directed at the American market? There is a whole range of policies and programs which, in the words of the Parliamentary Committee, are of fundamental importance to the maintenance of a distinctive Canadian identity or to keeping solemn commitments made to significant elements of Canadian society.
The issues to which I have referred should be spelled out very clearly at the outset. The Macdonald Commission has calculated the benefits of free trade but to date the Government has not provided us with an assessment of the costs by sector, by region, by industry and by worker. What will Canadian businesses and invididuals be asked to give up?
What about the footwear industry and the clothing industry? We all know that we are not going to get something for nothing through these negotiations. Is Canada going to lose entire industries as a result of the shift in economic activity? If so, which ones and where? What sort of adjustments to the system does the Government propose?
Has the Government explored all the alternatives to enhancing our economic performance? Some argue that the GATT process has already liberalized trade and that due to the complexity of our trading relationship with the United States, that process is the most effective way to increase our trade levels with the United States and other countries. Should we not, as the committee recommends, be concentrating first on settling existing irritants to trade with the United States, opening up informal discussions and setting up the parameters of these discussions with the United States? Should we not be listing the elements affected? Interprovincial trade needs to be examined and impediments removed.

As the House is aware, in November, 1984, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced a number of initiatives aimed at reducing Government expenditures. One
such initiative involved the decision to phase out Canagrex by April, 1985. This has been done. This Bill is intended to repeal the Canagrex Act and hence formally dissolve this Crown corporation.
It is a short Bill containing seven clauses. Its major feature, Clause 4, provides for all rights, property, obligations and liabilities of Canagrex to be the rights, property, obligations and liabilities of Her Majesty. For example, the contingent liability respecting the loan for sales to Cuba incurred by Canagrex is transformed into a liability of Her Majesty. Subclause 4(3) provides the specific authority for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to do all that is required in the winding up of the corporation. Section 100 of the Financial Administration Act provides that a Crown corporation may not be dissolved unless authorized by Parliament. The Canagrex Dissolution Act is meant to be such an authority.
Members will be pleased to know that positions were found or settlements made for all of the 30 staff of Canagrex, either in the public or the private sector. All operational files were turned over to the Department of Agriculture and measures have been taken by that Department, the Department of External Affairs and the Export Development Corporation to facilitate additional agricultural and food exports by the private sector.
As the Minister explained to the Standing Committee on Agriculture on December 18, 1984, it was obvious to all that Canagrex had start-up problems. While it undoubtedly would over time, have increased the volume of exports assisted, it was clear that Canagrex was not going to achieve the targets originally expected, nor was it going to be utilized by industry as planned. The activities provided for in the Canagrex Act were market identification and promotion, export counselling, provision of grants and contributions, state to state trading, loans and guarantees, the ability upon request to enter into joint ventures, and the power to import, export and buy and sell. Market identification missions, intelligence and analyses can and are being undertaken by both Agriculture Canada and External Affairs, as are market promotion activities, seminars and trade fairs. State to state trading, buying and selling and exporting may, if necessary, be undertaken through the Agricultural Products Board legislation. Grants and contributions are provided for under the PEMD food program of External Affairs. Insurance, loans and guarantees are available from the Export Development Corporation. Their services to the industry are in the process of being expanded. Cana-grex's export counselling and co-ordinating role will be undertaken by Agriculture Canada.
On March 1 1, 1985, Mr. Story, the President of Canagrex, appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture. In answer to a question as to who should co-ordinate and follow up the work started by Canagrex, he indicated his personal view that it should be Agriculture Canada. On June 20, 1985, the audit committee of the Board of Directors of Canagrex had a board meeting by way of a conference call in which a member of the Auditor General's office participated, and the report to the Minister on the financial statements of Canagrex
September 27, 1985

for the year ending March 31, 1985, was agreed to. These accounts indicated that for the year and Canagrex had a surplus of $1,846,278. Guarantees outstanding under the Cuban line of credit amounted to $8,311,728 as at March 31, 1985. These guarantees are to be assumed by the Department of Agriculture when the corporation is dissolved pursuant to Bill C-42. It should be noted that these guarantees will expire as of December 9, 1985. When proclaimed, Bill C-42 will result in the orderly liquidation of the corporation.
Canada's current financial situation demands action. The question was where within the agricultural portfolio cuts could be made that would be the least painful in both human and program impact. Canagrex fit such criteria. While painful, it is believed that the end result will be a streamlining and rationalization of agricultural and food exporting activities of the federal Government. The decision to wind up Canagrex was taken after a careful weighing of the factors involved and the impact such a decision would have on the agri-food sector. It should be stressed that the facilitating of additional exports of agricultural and food products continues to be a top priority of the Government. I believe that with the full co-operation of all federal Departments and agencies involved in facilitating export marketing, the private sector will be able to expand its exports on a more cost-effective basis.
I believe, as I know my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture does, that Bill C-42 is sound, desirable, and in the interests of Canadian agriculture and I urge Members on all sides of the House to support it.

country as the target for reduction in expenditures. It is striking that this has not only happened with this Government, but has characterized Governments that have got themselves into financial difficulty for 15 years in this country.

I believe it is a transfer that is badly misunderstood and the reason Governments pick out the family allowance and view it as a magnificent target when looking for ways to achieve economy.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member on his speech and the feeling he described about some of these very large constituencies. It is very difficult for any Members to serve constituents of such large ridings.
One of the principles we have at the present time in Section 42 of the Constitution of Canada talks about representation by population. This is a modified principle of representation by population that we have used all along. When I say modified, it refers to the base established by the number of Senate seats in any province. Apart from that, we have generally gone with representation by population. The more we see the urbanization of our country, the more we seem to be having problems in that regard. The rural ridings are getting bigger and bigger. The Hon. Member has just described how his constituency is already very large. How does he see reconciling on the one hand representation by population as a system in order to apportion the representation of this House while on the other hand trying to give some kind of a balance whereby we will not end up 20 years down the road with half a dozen members representing two-thirds of the physical land mass? Maybe we will not be quite that far, but we are certainly going in that direction.
In my own case, although my riding is much smaller, at one time in the past there was a Member for Glengarry, a Member for Prescott and a Member for Russell. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I represent all of Prescott, all of Russell, three-quarters of Glengarry and part of Ottawa-Carleton. That shows the shift of population and what is happening. I invite the Hon. Member to comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of the New Democratic Party to speak to this interesting Bill. Before doing so, I want to make a couple of comments. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) made a very powerful and interesting speech. For the record, I would like to associate myself and I believe my Party with the cause of Tina Malette. I hope that the Government and the Ambassador of Tunisia are listening and will be sent a copy of Hansard to see that there is unanimity in the House of Commons with respect to this issue.
Second, I want to take this opportunity to say personally, Godspeed and recovery to the Hon. Member for Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic (Mrs. Killens). She is a wonderful person and a great friend to all of us in the House. It would be nice if she were watching-I do not want her to become more sick by watching the House of Commons-and I hope she will get better and return to the House quickly. I believe that hope is shared by all Members.
Let me make some remarks about the Bill and the speech made by the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby). I wanted to hear some facts and figures from the Hon. Member for Halifax West but they were given by the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I believe it is necessary to have more detailed facts on the number of missing children to determine the number missing as a result of a family situation, a non-family situation or whether it is a poor family home situation where the child seems to have run away.
I attempted to find those facts in the Badgley Commission but there is not much information with respect to the problem of using the police power to return missing children as proposed by the Hon. Member in his Bill.
I certainly agree with the Hon. Member that it must be a terrible experience to be a parent of a missing child. As I listened to the speech by the Hon. Member for Halifax West, it appeared that there is a grass roots movement to deal with
Missing Children Search Act
this problem as often happens in Canadian society. Members will recall the group called MADD. These were people against impaired drivers. They campaigned for tougher penalties because some of their family members had been victims of impaired drivers. They began to pressure Members of Parliament. They were not represented by any funded group, business or labour body. They were ordinary Canadians who were concerned about this problem.
Members of Parliament did receive a letter from a group called The Victims of Violence and I thank them for writing to us. We appreciate the kind of grass roots nature of this group. I will come back to that in a minute.
The Hon. Member for Halifax West says that the police do not respond as quickly to missing children as they do to missing cars and boats. That is a pretty sad thing. I cannot believe, although one notes the concern with property in our society, that that is the situation. The Hon. Member tells we there is no list of missing children but there is a list of missing cars and boats. I agree with him that that sounds wrong and it is terrible. He said that to be missing is not a crime. He is right. This is one part of his Bill I did not understand. Perhaps when it gets to committee the point will be clarified. Is this an amendment to the Criminal Code or not? I think it should be, and it should not stand as a separate Bill. If it becomes an amendment to the Criminal Code, there are certain aspects of the Bill we should look at very closely. We have to balance our concern against missing children and the ability to do something in terms of an investigation and in getting the children back.
Some of the wording in his Bill is not crystal clear. I know he said that this was a general approach to flag he issue and to keep pressure on so that something will be done. I have looked at Clauses 6 and 7 of the Bill. Clause 6 calls for a person to advise the Minister in writing that a police officer has refused to assist in the search for a missing child and that the Minister may order the police officer to take certain actions. In Clause 7 there can be a search warrant to search premises and so on when people suspect a missing child is involved. This goes a little far, and there are some civil liberties concerns here. Do we want to give the police that kind of power? Can that kind of power be abused? We have to weigh that against the concern of getting the bureacracy, and I include the police, to pay more concern to missing children as opposed to missing cars and boats.
The Hon. Member said that 1.5 million children went missing each year in the Unites States.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to enter into this debate. There is an interesting question with respect to whether or not the Coast Guard station in my constituency is the most southerly in Canada. I think it probably is. Partly for that reason I felt it important to add my voice to the concerns which have been raised by some of my colleagues with respect to the introduction of user-pay principles in the provision of Coast Guard services.
Coast Guard services with respect to my constituency are of special and particular concern because of their connection with the tourist industry. The tourist industry has been identified by local economic development groups as the area in which we see economic expansion and job growth in our community. In fact, we find a great many people who come across the inland waterways in the Essex County area to take advantage of tourist opportunities on the Canadian side, both in Lake St. Clair and in the Detroit River. I fear that if we institute a system of fees which could be applied to pleasure boats this could become a serious disincentive to those people who make the choice to take advantage of the tourist facilities on our side of the water system in which people have invested.
I raise a point which has been stressed by my colleague from Regina with respect to philosophically questioning the idea of user-pay. I think it is fair to say that in the country we have a history of transportation infrastructure which is in place and which was built by the community for the community. It is something which has contributed to the development of our country. At this stage in our history the putting into effect of an alien principle, a principle outside of our traditions, needs to be closely examined. We cannot examine the matter closely with respect to this Bill because the details of how the user-pay principle would be implemented are not spelled out.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that 1 rise to speak in the debate on Bill C-224, an Act respecting the national hymn of Canada. It is a great honour for me to speak on the Bill which was introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), for whom 1 have nothing but the greatest respect. It is also appropriate to congratulate the Hon. Member for introducing this important Bill since it gave me the chance to explore the question of national symbols as I sought to inform myself for this discussion. I might mention that in my research I had the good fortune to come across the transcript of a broadcast interview carried out by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and, as it happens, it was with the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills.
I would like to say at the outset that I thought it was admirably candid of the Hon. Member to acknowledge the fact that the inspiration for the hymn came not from him but from one of his constituents, Dr. Kenneth Hicken, a professor at the University of Lethbridge. He composed the music and wrote the lyrics. It was translated into French by another University of Lethbridge professor, Dr. Gaston R. Renaud. His admission came in response to a question which I suspect is common to many Canadians, namely, why do we need a national hymn in this country? The Hon. Member replied in these words, and I quote:
Well, I think Dr. Hicken hit the nail on the head when this country's come through some real tough times ... and so he simply decided that what he needed, in view of the moral situation of the country, and the East-West antipathies, and the French-English problems ... that we needed to have a national hymn to remind us that there's more to living than just our own lives-
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, when Professor Hicken got to thinking about the need for a national hymn, he sat down and composed one.
In that CBC interview, the Hon. Member suggested that for very special, solemn occasions-particularly if the Queen were here-Canada could have what he called a triad of God Save the Queen, our national anthem, O Canada, and the national hymn. He suggested its use would be limited to times of national crisis when we are trying to bring people together. A national emergency, perhaps, or wartime, would be an appropriately important time to have a national hymn. He went on to say that while our national anthem is excellent, and the proposed hymn is in no way intended to supplant it, there are occasions where you would want something more solemn,
October 18, 1985

something along the lines of when the Americans employ their hymn America the Beautiful. It would, he said, be a kind of companion to the national anthem.
The Hon. Member said he is pleasantly surprised at the number of people who support the idea of a national hymn and indicated that while he is proud of the Hicken hymn, he feels that, if the Government and Parliament favour the principle of a national hymn, it might be well to open the matter to a country-wide submission of hymns. He foresaw a sort of hymn-writing competition, and it is here that I am strongly in agreement with the Hon. Member. I am one who is enormously stirred by the strains of O Canada sung sincerely, and I trust Canadians of whatever descent will never cease to respond with pride to our anthem.
A national anthem, like a national flag, is an important external symbol of nationhood. I had the pleasure, as a backbencher in a previous Parliament, of introducing a Private Members' Bill to have O Canada recognized as Canada's official national anthem. Of course, as a back-bencher in the Opposition that did not happen, but I had the honour of being the official spokesman for the Conservative Party. The Government of the day brought in legislation which finally brought the idea to fruition.
I feel, however, that the words to O Canada have not been publicized enough and a lot more should be done. I also feel the need for more songs celebating our land. It is at this point that I would venture to offer a refinement to my hon. colleague. Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to offer some thoughts on the matter before us today, particularly because the broadcasting of parliamentary business makes such a positive contribution to the Canadian political process, indeed to Canadian identity.
However, while any attempt to improve television coverage of parliamentary proceedings is certainly worth while, 1 have some doubts about the motion before us. The motion proposes that the Government should consider the advisability of recommending to the CBC the feasibility of rebroadcasting the daily proceedings of the House of Commons. It might be helpful to outline how the CBC provides national distribution of its parliamentary service and the role it plays in doing so.
The House of Commons broadcast service, which comes under your direct responsibility, Mr. Speaker, as you well know, provides the video and audio signals to any broadcaster who wishes to distribute them. The CBC is licensed by the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission to carry on a network operation for the distribution of these proceedings. The CBC's parliamentary television network takes the signals, packages them and uplinks them for satellite distribution to cable companies across Canada in both official languages. Cable operators may then receive and carry the service at their own discretion. The CBC does not have an exclusive licence to distribute these proceedings, but it is the only national distributor at this time. In doing so, it provides a valuable service to Canadians and contributes immeasurably to fulfilling the objectives set out for the CBC in the Broadcasting Act.
The fundamental questions raised by this motion are: Do Canadians want the additional service? Would they watch it if they had it? I believe that before we advise the Government to extend this service it would make sense to ask Canadians if they want it. Broadcasting parliamentary procedures at present costs Canadians $2.5 million to $3 million per year. Most of us would agree that money spent on familiarizing Canadians with their Government is money well spent. Broadcasting Parliament's procedures give Canadians an opportunity to better understand their Government and how it operates. As today's article in The Gazette notes, these broadcasts reach literally thousands if not millions of people across Canada and the continent. For the past eight years this service has served an important function in educating and informing Canadians on their Government. However, before we undertake an extension of the service, I believe we must be absolutely certain that it is wanted. As elected representatives we must ensure that tax dollars are spent wisely and with the public interest in mind. This holds true for the CBC as it does for other Crown corporations. Let me point to an example which illustrates the need for proper management of tax dollars consistent with the wishes of Canadians.
As many Members may be aware, the CBC is planning to build a new broadcast centre in Metropolitan Toronto. When plans for the new building were prepared CBC officials selected a site in downtown Toronto and proceeded to estimate construction costs. In March of this year the City of Scarborough made a proposal to the CBC for construction of this centre in Scarborough which could save Canadian taxpayers over $90 million. The CBC resisted this proposal and has continued to insist that the centre must be located in downtown Toronto. Fortunately, the persistent efforts of members
October 24, 1985

of Scarborough Council, Scarborough Development officials and Members of Parliament from Scarborough have focused public attention on this issue and called into question the selection of this downtown site. I raise this question to point out to Members the importance of analysing motions like this which ask the Government to extend services which Canadians may not want and cannot afford.
Before we extend this service perhaps we should better inform Canadians of the existing service which is available. I am sure Members from all sides are continually informing their constituents as to when parliamentary proceedings are broadcast in their area. The simple fact is that many Canadians are not even aware that they can watch these proceedings. Many of those who do want to tune in are forced to purchase a converter to do so. With all due respect to the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), I think the motion itself is not the ideal mechanism for tendering our suggestion for enhancing television coverage of the House of Commons. That opportunity will occur when we discuss the recommendations made by the Special Committee on Reform of the House of Commons. Indeed, in its report that committee suggested that the distribution of the House of Commons broadcast service might be improved, and mentioned that one idea might be to repeat the proceedings at a time when the potential audience is larger.

Mr. Speaker, you ask whether the House is ready for the question. I am certainly not ready for the question. A number of Members on this side of the House want to make a contribution to the debate on this legislation. I want to assure you that the House will not be ready for the question for some time.
The Bill before the House today concerns employment equity, or affirmative action. Let me commence by briefly explaining the importance of affirmative action and why we are urging the Government to implement a positive and effective affirmative action program. Affirmative action is fundamental to our values in a society which firmly believes in equality of opportunity and condition. Since we value the opportunity for people to participate in society as a whole, our citizens must have the fullest opportunity to develop as individuals and the community must have access to the full potential of its human resources. We do not want to see anyone in our society excluded from that participation. It is only on the basis of each person being given an opportunity to develop and become productive in society that we can have a community in which we can have pride and a sense of security.
Affirmative action is a means of confirming our value of equality in Canadian life. It has long been stated that Canadian society is far from equal and that a number of groups in Canadian society are far from reaching that goal of equality.
I want to refer to the status of women in our society. One glaring example of inequality is the fact that for each dollar earned by men, women earn only 60 cents. While women have
October 31, 1985

made significant advances in employment in the last couple of decades, the remuneration they receive is inadequate and far less than what a man would receive in similar circumstances. We must address this problem through affirmative action. Furthermore, it follows that women's pensions will be 60 per cent of the pension of their male counterparts. The vast majority of Canadians are not willing to tolerate this kind of inequality.
We have in our society a number of visible minorities, including black and Asian people.
The inequality of visible minorities in Canada is a worry which I am sure many Canadians have when they look south across the border and see what has happened with the black people, particularly in the cities. Not only to see the potential of individuals fulfilled, but also to see that our communities are ones in which we can live in peace, comfort and enjoyment, it is important that visible minorities be given full opportunity, particularly in the area of employment.
The same inequality exists for the handicapped. The handicapped are in many ways excluded from our society by architecture because few buildings are accessible to the handicapped, a situation that needs to be changed. Buildings are only a symbol of the way we bar access to equal opportunity for handicapped individuals. Other changes are needed, changes in employment policies and in recruitment procedures. What about opportunities for training? The vast majority of Canadians would like the Government to take effective action to ensure that handicapped people have equal access to opportunity and employment and to see that society benefits from the rich resources of the handicapped.
Another group of people who stand out in terms of inequality and call upon us to establish effective affirmative action programs are the native people. If we look at native people in the poor areas of cities, such as Winnipeg and other western cities, we find that poverty is intolerable. It is visible. People live in inadequate housing and have a low level of education. Unemployment is in the area of 60 per cent. These are not official statistics but educated guesses. If we look at native people in rural areas on reserves, we find that unemployment is in the area of 80 per cent to 90 per cent. Greater equality is needed.
The need for affirmative action is based upon lack of equality. Most Canadians want a society in which people have equality of opportunity and human condition.
This Bill before the House falls far short of what could be called effective affirmative action. The Bill is a voluntary program rather than a mandatory one. We know from the United States experience and from our own experience here with regard to voluntary programs that we need a mandatory program with deadlines, goals and specific objectives.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom):
Employment Equity
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
Bill C-62, an Act respecting Employment Equity be not now read a second
time but that it be read a second time this day six months hence.
I move this motion, Mr. Speaker, because the Government needs more time to find out about why this Bill falls far short of an adequate affirmative action program. The Government needs to rethink its position. We need the six months for the Government to come up with an effective affirmative action program.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-62 and on the motion moved by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper).
This employment equity Bill is really a missed opportunity. Because that is so, we in the New Democratic Party have great difficulty supporting it. There are several reasons for that difficulty. The Bill really calls for a voluntary program, which is clearly unacceptable to my Party.
Voluntary affirmative action programs have been tried in several jurisdictions other than in Canada-most notably, in the United States, Germany and other European countries- and it was found that they simply did not work. In the United States, in particular, it was decided in the 1960s to come forward with mandatory programs, which have proven to be quite effective.
I, along with other Members from all sides of the House, had the opportunity in 1980, after the election campaign, to form an all-Party committee of the House of Commons to look into problems affecting the disabled population. We came up with a number of recommendations which, if implemented, could have been of great assistance to disabled Canadians in their attempt to participate in the mainstream of Canadian society.
I would like to centre my remarks on the disabled community rather than on women, natives or other groups as other members of my caucus have already addressed themselves to those groups. The committee recognized that most of the problems affecting the disabled community centred on the key issue of employment opportunity. One can talk about the social needs of that particular group in any terms one wishes, whether it be in terms of access to housing, access to transportation, education, recreation, information or even technical aids. These things cannot be separated one from the other. Each one is connected to the other. One cannot talk about providing an individual with access to education on all levels including post-secondary education without also talking about how that individual can be productively employed following the receipt of his or her education, and this is assuming that the individual can get into the educational system to begin with.
As the committee went across the country speaking to Canadians, it heard numerous stories indicating that there are literally thousands of children who are denied access to education because of their disabilities. This Bill does not address
Employment Equity
that problem. It does not address training opportunities for people who happened to be disabled. Unless we talk about that in a very real and concrete way, we cannot talk about employment opportunities because one is synonymous with the other.
We cannot talk about employment opportunities without talking about how we allow the individual to be moved from the place of residence to the place of employment. It must be recognized that most modes of transportation are not designed to be used by physically disabled people. We have to talk about these things in a very real and basic way. This Bill does not do that. It does not even touch upon that.
I find it surprising that the Government would introduce a measure like this. The Canadian Automobile Association states that the high cost of gasoline has been a major culprit in deterring foreign travellers from auto touring in Canada. About 85 per cent of all tourism in Canada is by automobile.

The tourist industry is definitely pessimistic. We could take steps to reverse the trend in this crucial sector, and we would be well advised to start by reducing the federal tax on gasoline.

Speech:
Last September 19, Mr. Speaker, a very strong earthquake hit Mexico, and we all know the aftermath. According to estimates, 8,000 people died in this tragedy and 30,000 more were injured. Material destruction was widespread-thousands of homes, schools, hospitals. Given the extent of the catastrophy, the international community rallied to provide help.
Mr. Speaker, I think that all Members of the House can be proud of Canada's quick response to this tragedy. Less than 36 hours after the earthquake, the Canadian Government had announced a $1 million contribution for emergency assistance through the Canadian International Development Agency, CIDA. Without delay, we sent to Mexico a cargo of essential equipment along with expert staff. On September 24, we
announced an additional $250,000 contribution to a fund administered by our embassy in Mexico and reserved for small assistance projects. I should think that Canadians who had close relatives or friends in Mexico were also grateful for the exceptional efforts made by Department of External Affairs consular personnel to find people from whom no news had been received and to assist our fellow Canadians who needed help.

Last September, Mr. Speaker, I indicated that the Government would address itself to the matter of providing longer term aid as well. While the film crews are gone from Mexico, our determination to assist those in need remains. It is for the purpose of reporting to the House on that aspect of our work that I wish to speak today.

Our first task was to assess the needs and, to that end, Canada worked in close co-operation with Mexico. As soon as the Mexican Government knew what its priorities were with respect to long-term reconstruction, a Canadian planning mission was sent to Mexico. This team was made up of representatives of two Canadian non-governmental organizations, a spokesman for the business world, and CIDA officials. The members of the mission met with officials of various Mexican Government levels. We also consulted other donor countries, multilateral institutions, private interests and Mexican NGOs.
Mr. Speaker, following these discussions and an assessment of requirements, I am happy to announce that the Government of Canada will be using CIDA budgets to allocate an additional $3,750,000 for aid to Mexico. Areas that will benefit from this assistance-again, further to the discussions we had with the Mexican authorities-are education, housing and health.
The funds will be distributed as follows: first, one million dollars will be spent to rebuild and equip facilities on the campus of the National College for Technical and Professional Training, where a building collapsed, causing numerous casualties among the student population.
Second, I am happy to announce that CIDA will set aside one million dollars for the reconstruction of low-cost housing units and community facilities.
These funds will be channelled through Canadian NGOs under the auspices of the Canadian Council for International Co-operation. The project will be carried out in the most severely stricken communities, in co-operation with Mexican community agencies.
Third, we are allocating the sum of one million dollars for a rural health and pure water project, to be carried out by UNICEF in Guerrero State, which sufferred considerable damage. Beneficiaries of this project will be the peasants in the many isolated communities in this State.
Fourth, a special allocation of $500,000 will be set aside to cope with any additional requests we may receive within these

November 7, 1985

three areas. Finally, an additional $250,000 will be made available to the Canadian Embassy for its small projects program. Experience has shown that this is an ideal way to respond to immediate construction needs.
Yesterday, our embassy's management committee, which met to approve the initial series of projects, was already proceeding to identify specific projects. These will include rebuilding a primary school, a nursery school, a shelter for young girls and a community co-operative for manufacturing bricks.
These new contributions raise the total value of our aid to Mexico for both emergency assistance and long-term reconstruction to $5 million. I might add that this was done in under 50 days.
Canadians have a very special feeling of solidarity for this hospitable country which remains one of their favourite holiday destinations. Once again, Canada has proven to be true to its humanitarian traditions. 1 must say that it is indeed an honour for me to represent it whenever the time comes for assistance to be provided to countries and people in need.

And I want to pay tribute to all those who made it possible for us to act effectively in such difficult circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise today to address an issue of concern expressed to me on numerous occasions. The complaint is that changes to the 1978 firearms control law adversely affect the ownership and use of recreational firearms.

First, it illustrates how all of us can participate in ways that are helpful to the environment. Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief comment in rebuttal to the very interesting perspective which the Hon. Member has placed on the NEP. If one were sitting in Atlantic Canada listening to the Hon. Member, one would have to conclude that all those years of Liberal Government gratuities given to the part of Canada he represents, indeed to all of Canada, should have produced a great increase in employment and a strong surge in our economy. Indeed, if the Liberal approach of liberally taking money from private sector pockets and redistributing it to other parts of the country had worked, we would not have seen unemployment rise from one million people in 1980 to 1.5 million by the time that Government left office in 1984.
We agree that benefits were delivered to provinces and regions such as Cape Breton which the Hon. Member represents. However, if we were to plot on a graph the data regarding the transfer of funds to the Atlantic provinces under Liberal programs and the impact on unemployment and the health of the economy, the level of disposable income and the new economic initiatives by private interests in that region, we would find the results were inversely proportional to the assistance given. That is, the more money we pumped in by way of Liberal Government hand-outs, the more unemployment increased. As the Government in Ottawa mounted a
major war with the Atlantic provinces, particularly Newfoundland, unemployment continued to rise.
The Hon. Member asked us to show what improvements in the economy this Government has brought about in the 14 months it has been in office. Over the last 14 months, more than 300,000 jobs were created, bringing unemployment down to 1.1 million from 1.5 million under the Trudeau regime. That is the evidence that the private sector incentive driven approach is far superior to the Liberal approach of taking money from one region of Canada and handing it out holus-bolus in the form of grants to another region.
This Government does indeed take a new approach. It places the incentives in the hands of those who can take greatest advantage of them. That is the purpose of the $250 million of drilling incentives to be made available annually. This will ensure the pace of offshore drilling in his region, and ensure that the benefits are returned to the people of those regions through the private companies and individuals who will make such investments.
In conclusion, let me say that the Hon. Member tended to mislead this House when he implied that Members sitting on the Government side today did not resist vehemently the Draconian and confiscatory nature of the NEP. If he consults Hansard and the record of the debates on Bill C-48, the Canada Lands Act, if he would consult in particular the record of committee hearings in response to the budgetary measures flowing from the NEP, he would find indeed that members of this Government resisted most vocally not only the goals and objectives of the NEP, but the very divisive and impudent way in which it was foisted upon this country by the Government of which he was a part. I would ask the Hon. Member to clarify for the record that indeed it was the outspoken objection on the part of members of this Party that led to an unprecedented overthrow of a Government and its replacement with one which is devoted to creating a stronger economy and thousands and thousands of new jobs.

Mr. Speaker, although Justice Jules Deschenes' decision on the taking of Soviet evidence has outlined several safeguards, it has ignored safeguards which must be in place before any agreement is reached.
Justice Deschenes makes no mention of the right of the accused to be represented by counsel and to receive notice. The slightest deviation from the conditions set out should immediately nullify the agreement. There can be no allowance for the taking of evidence by anyone other than Canadian authorities. Justice Deschenes' conclusion that, barring unforeseen circumstances, the evidence be elicited by deputy commissioners leaves the door wide open for Soviet authorities to impede the justice procedure.
The rights of Canadians must be protected, and every guarantee protecting those rights must be in writing. It is not enough to say that the Commission will insist that they be accepted and observed. All the conditions must be accepted in writing and observed, or they will not be worth the paper they are written on.

In keeping with Departmental guidelines that are available to the public, the facts presented by both the investigator and the two pilots will be reviewed by a third party.
