Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a statement on the tragic deaths of a young Canadian mother and her infant son. Although we are awaiting formal identification by the husband and father, our information is that Mrs. Valinda Leonard and her infant son, Andrew, of Beiseker, Alberta, were killed in the hijacking of the Egyptian airliner to Malta. I wish to express my own deepest condolences and those of the Government and of the people of Canada to her family. I also, Sir, want to pay tribute to the manner in which the family has responded to the stress and tragedy of this weekend.

November 25, 1985
Statements by Ministers
No nation is immune to the scourge of terrorism. Two innocent Canadians now join the list of victims of this international brutality. The Government of Canada condemns the hijacking of the Egyptian airliner and profoundly regrets the tragic loss of life which ensued. This most recent incident again demonstrates the urgent need for concerted international action to combat acts of terrorism. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) raised this issue before the United Nations General Assembly. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) has proposed changes affecting international air travel.
With our friends and allies Canada is pursuing other concrete measures to combat terrorism. Senior officials of my Department will be meeting in Bonn on December 10 and 11 to continue consultations with our Summit Seven partners. We will continue to pursue vigorously all available means to eliminate the scourge of terrorism and to bring to justice the perpetrators of these brutal acts.

This action is currently under way at a total cost of some $8 million and will continue and be accelerated as required.

ate action can be taken, such measures will be implemented. The nature of these cannot be determined until the results of the study are in hand.

Mr. Speaker, as the Official Opposition critic dealing with policies and regulations regarding the handicapped, it is my privilege to comment on the statement just made by the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Blais-Grenier). Along with other Members of the House, I congratulate her on any new steps she

November 26, 1985

may have taken in the ongoing process of establishing equal opportunities for the handicapped to have full access to transportation, and for the elimination of physical and attitudinal barriers to travel. However, I gather that some Members of the Standing Committee on Transport, which is touring the country and taking evidence, are puzzled as to why the Minister did not wait to make her statement until tomorrow when they would be back in Ottawa and able to be present.
I said that I welcomed any signs of progress and I have listened carefully to her statement. Mr. Speaker, I had to listen carefully because, regrettably, there is precious little in her statement that shows progress or that is new since either the press release of her immediate predecessor six months ago or since the progress report made by the last Liberal Government in 1983 entitled Surmounting Obstacles. The Minister said that now is the time for action and then she proceeded to give us 10 action steps. However, of the 10 steps she cited, eight of them appeared in her predecesor's news release of six months ago and she has repeated them almost word for word. Of the two items that are new, neither of them are action oriented but are announcements of more committees and conferences, important though they are. Basically there is no new action at all except with regard to the announcement of 25 communities which will later learn what will be coming to them.
Regrettably, what we heard was not a statement by a Minister to bring some new developments to the attention of the House, but just one more in a long series of attempts by the Government to try to take something which was an initiative undertaken during the last Liberal Government, dress it up in a Tory blue wrapper and call it, as she has done, a new policy. It is too bad that they do not leave well enough alone, give credit where credit is due and get on with new and further action. It seems that the Conservatives just cannot bring themselves to lead, to set the example and to act. All they can do is to lick the bullet-they just cannot bring themselves to bite it.
As far back as 1980 the Parliament of Canada established a special committee on the disabled and the handicapped to review the scope of federal programs in the area of disability. In 1981 it made its report called Obstacles which contained 130 recommendations to improve the status of disabled and handicapped Canadians. Action progress was monitored by this committee and subsequent reports showed that by 1983 the Government had dealt with two-thirds of the recommendations and with three-quarters of those dealing with transportation.
While the Canadian Government did much in the past to deal with such matters within its jurisdiction, and should have done even more, the fact is that the real door to equality for the handicapped was thrown open by the passage of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms by the last Liberal Government. That, Mr. Speaker, is what will ultimately force all those who provide public service to give equal access to the
Statements by Ministers
handicapped and that is what will propel the Government to some action.
Thanks to the Charter, thanks to the courts, thanks to a decision by a Saskatchewan court last June, and thanks to the Supreme Court for its decision not to allow an appeal, a key principle in this regard was established. Now the handicapped across Canada can demand that appropriate measures be taken to ensure that equal access becomes a reality. Because of the Charter the courts say that identical treatment is not necessarily equal treatment and, therefore, special steps must be taken in any public place to give equal access to the handicapped. It is because of the Charter that the Government must be made to act. It must not be allowed to wait for the courts to settle every case. It must be forced to be bold, to make regulations and to pass laws.
The Minister talked about "developing a detailed strategy" in her blueprint for action, "clarification of procedures", "encouraging negotiation", "working in a spirit of consensus and co-operation", "appointing task forces", and "finalizing guidelines". That is hardly what we would call the language of resolute and vigorous action, Mr. Speaker. What is more, the Minister of State for Transport (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) has not announced any minimum standards. She has not announced any timetable. She has not announced any figures showing financial commitment. She has only recycled an old press release.
Laurie Beachell, National Co-ordinator for the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped, COPOH, says that instead of vague guidelines detailed standards are needed to force compliance. David Blaker, Executive Director of the Advocacy Research Centre for the Handicapped in Toronto, says that they need to be made law. We still do not hear from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government that they will bring in standards, regulations and laws because they do not believe in that sort of thing. Why did the Government not bring in an immediate response to the equality rights report and fulfil recommendations 48 and 49 of that report? That could have been done today. The Government does not want to regulate. It prefers to deregulate.
It is precisely because the Tories lick the bullet instead of biting it that today, tomorrow and, regrettably, for some time to come, many disabled people will be refused transportation and will be discriminated against. Speech:
1 do not mind answering questions, Mr. Speaker, if they warrant a response. I would simply point out to the Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence that the report he is referring to was not a report written by that special committee. It is a report written by the Liberal Government in response to the Obstacles Report. That special committee tore that response to shreds. We called witnesses before the committee. They were people who were disabled consumers. We asked them for their response to the Government's response to our report. In nearly every instance, the response we received from organizations like the Canadian Council of the Deaf, COPOH and a host of other disabled consumer organizations was that the Government did not do what it said it did.
The Government gave a response that was based more on a public relations exercise than in responding in real terms to the recommendations in that report. That is all I want to say on that subject because when we enter into debate in this House we should be concerned with facts, not on what someone would like to believe happened.
Let me deal with the Minister's statement. As I pointed out, the Minister is relatively new in that portfolio and I want to be charitable. I will say that at least the Minister made a report to the House, which previous Ministers have not done. I appreciate that response, rather than those we received from the previous Government. I appreciate the Minister giving us the opportunity to speak in the House on a matter of grave concern to a large percentage of the Canadian population who are disabled or handicapped. Ten per cent may be considered a rather conservative number but at least 10 per cent of the Canadian population are considered to be disabled or handicapped.
Transportation is very much a key to allowing disabled Canadians to participate fully in the mainstream of Canadian life. Employment is the number one key to making a disabled person a fully functional and integrated member of Canadian society but there is not much sense talking about creating jobs for disabled individuals unless we can provide the means for getting those people from their home to their workplace and back again. I am afraid that the Minister's proposals will not achieve that goal.
Unfortunately, today the Minister only gave more suggestions for study, apart from a couple of areas. I commend the Minister for setting up the pilot project in Newfoundland. That was a key demand from COPOH during the election campaign. The Government promised to do something about it and I am glad it has acted.
November 26, 1985

However, there are many other areas that should have been addressed more progressively and with greater leadership than what the Minister has done today. For example, there is absolutely no question that the disabled have not yet realized equality in transportation. Last weekend the executive of COPOH met in the City of Ottawa. At least two disabled members of that executive had difficulty with their air transportation. Air Canada gave one member, who came from Cape Breton to Ottawa, a hard time about getting on the aircraft simply because that person was disabled.
In the time I have remaining, I want to point out to the Minister that she did not talk about taxi service. There is absolutely nothing that requires a taxi service from an airport, which is regulated and licensed by the federal Government, to accommodate the needs of a disabled person. I would ask her to take that into consideration in her statement to the House.
We welcome the suggestion by the Minister that there will be an international conference in Vancouver next year. I do not know whether it is simply an oversight by the Minister, but she said that the groups that will be involved in that international conference will be experts from Government, industry and the academic community. 1 want to suggest strongly to the Minister that there are no other people who are more expert in this field than the disabled. They must be involved in that conference. That was the whole purpose of the International Year of the Disabled. They are the experts.
In conclusion, I ask the Minister to consider that very seriously and come back to the House to give us the assurance that the disabled will be involved in that conference.

December 6, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
proposed an increase to 289. In fact, I agree with the Hon. Member of Lac-Saint-Jean that an increase of seven seats is acceptable. This would reflect what happened in the Committee and it is therefore more acceptable for those of us who sat on the Committee.

British Columbia will have two, and so will Alberta and Ontario. I do not want to be a bad sport and to seem envious of these provinces which are to receive additional seats. I am going to try and speak as calmly as possible without making any partisan comments.
As it is often pointed out, Quebec is not like other provinces. That Province is the centre of French culture in Canada, and as such, whenever there have been redistributions, debates centering on the redistribution of seats, that point always has came up. And it must do so once again.
I say without being chauvinistic, it is clear that Quebec has a special role in Canada. It is the anchor point of the Frenchspeaking community. Furthermore it is the critical mass of the French-speaking community in Canada. I say it is the anchor point because minorities outside Quebec expect the latter to remain strong, because if Quebec does not survive as an entity, that is the end of the French-speaking community in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak today about an important problem which affects more than 17,000 women each year in Canada, including 7,000 in Quebec. I wish to call the attention of the House to the breast implant studies submitted to me a few weeks ago by Dr. Robert Guidoin, an eminent researcher at the Experimental Surgery Department of the Universite Laval in Sainte-Foy.
As a woman, I am very sensitive to this serious issue, which jeopardizes the health of many Canadian women each year. I made a statement about this last week and asked a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to
find out what had been done following my many interventions in this regard.
If I raise this issue once more today, it is because I consider that all Members of this House should be made aware of the urgency of undertaking a vast study program on breast implants used by surgeons, and especially on the need to regulate the quality of these implants.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the Department of National Health and Welfare now provides no control over silicone implants used by surgeons.
Research clearly show that, during the two years following the initial operation, inadequate silicone implants can rupture or leak, causing considerable damage to the tissue of the patient who must then be hospitalized for additional surgery.
Mr. Speaker, the optimism with which the use of medical silicones was greeted has now been tempered by caution in view of the various types of evolutive complications associated with them, such as calcification, distortion and proliferating encapsulation.
Of the implants examined, 21.7 per cent have shown signs of encapsulation, and this does not take into account the fibrous capsules sent by themselves. A slight difference was noted between intact and damaged implants. Intact implants showed fewer fibrous capsules, or 13.9 per cent, than the damaged ones, which showed 38.2 per cent.
As for mineralization, it was found present not only in the fibrous capsules, but even on the very surface of the implants. Of all implants examined, 48.1 per cent showed mineralization of the implant itself and 11.8 per cent of the fibrous capsule. The conclusions of the analyses show that intact specimens seemed to be more mineralized than the damaged ones. The proportion was 50 per cent in the first case and 40 per cent in the second. In addition, implants of the Heyer Schulte brand showed 80 per cent mineralization compared with 38.1 per cent for Dow Corning brands.

In my experience as a Member, Mr. Speaker, I often came across similar cases, for example respecting old age security pensions, where cheques were still being addressed to the names of retired people after death. Rule No. 2 of the Act, which is now being amended by the Bill before us, reads as follows:
Subject to Rules 5(2) and (3), there shall be assigned to a large province a number of members equal to the number obtained by dividing the population of the large province by the electoral quotient of Quebec.
In the following rules, there are provisions for small provinces and intermediate provinces, but it is quite clear that representation from Quebec with 75 Members, or 79 Members in recognition of the population growth in that vital province, was the very cornerstone of the distributional structure of the House of Commons.
What do we find in the new Bill that is before us, the Bill which we want to send back to committee for further consideration? We find that Rule 1 of Subsection 51(1) of the Constitution Act, 1867, is to be amended as follows:

December 17, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
There shall be assigned to each of the provinces a number of members equal to the number obtained by dividing the total population of the provinces by two hundred and seventy-nine and by dividing the population of each province by the quotient so obtained, counting any remainder in excess of 0.50 as one after the said process of division.
This is the cancellation of a fundamental principle that has prevailed in Canadian Confederation since its very beginning. This is a declaration that the House of Commons shall contain about 280 Members and that the total population of the country shall be divided simply by the number 279 to arrive at a figure which will then be divided into the population of each of the provinces. Of course, in the next stage will come the further nuances which will be necessary to make the system work.
I marvel that a Government with the kind of strength it has in the Province of Quebec-or is it actually strength-would do a thing like that. I would say that a preceding Conservative Government, the one of 1957 to 1963 led by the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker, was not known for having very much sensitivity to the aspiration of Quebec. To have had the Diefenbaker Government do a thing like this would not have astonished me at all. However, it seems quite astonishing that this Government would change the cornerstone of our system of representation which is based on the Province of Quebec and replace it with a numerical system which has one concern alone and that is to hold down the growth of the Canadian Parliament.
This concern over the growth of the House of Commons is supposedly based on the cost involved in increasing the size of the House of Commons. This leads us to wonder whether the expenditures we incur in representing our constituents are regarded as wasted money. If we were to facilitate the representation of people in isolated communities and make it easy for the citizens who live in my riding to be in touch with me, would it be money wasted? It seems to me that at some point, we would gain to move toward tyranny. What Conservative Members said many a time about the application of closure by the preceding Liberal Government is what Conservative Government members are in fact on the brink of doing. When they suggest that money spent for additional Members of Parliament who would provide good representation in money lost, they are not very far away from saying that all of our deliberations are rather a waste of money. I recognize, however, that that may be a long way away.
There have been seven impositions of closure in just a few weeks on matters that have had precious little debate in the House of Commons. We have a small Opposition which is using a six month hoist motion in order to renew its opportunity to debate these matters and keep them before the public so that we may discover whether or not the people of Canada are critical of measures the Government wants to put through. We see Government members reacting to these attempts to keep matters before the Canadian public in this way even though they themselves are past masters at it. When we see this Government, which has been in office only 15 months and
some days, acting in this kind of high-handed and authoritative manner, then surely everything Government members ever said to the last Liberal Government about tyrannical tendencies is fairly enough applied to them.
The consideration of fundamental changes to our Constitution is being pushed through by closure. What is one to say about a Government that behaves that way?

I do not want to take too long making my comments because I understand that many other Hon. Members want to say a few words about this motion. I would like to give them the opportunity to do so.
The question of Cyprus and its invasion by Turkey has been raised in the House several times by Hon. Members on all sides of the House, including the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) and the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn.). They were quite convinced that they could do so again provided they were given the opportunity to make their own decisions on their own behalf without a strong military presence on the island.
This is the eleventh year since the Turkish invasion of Cyprus; 11 years since Turkey sent its army to occupy 40 per cent of Cyprus and displace one-third of its population or some 200,000 persons. Turkey also captured thousands of defenceless civilians and shot, butchered or raped hundreds and 2,000 of these are still missing. Turkey then brought in a flood of colonists from mainland Turkey to whom the stolen properties of the displaced refugees were handed over. Despite worldwide condemnation of this action by the United Nations General Assembly, the European Common Market and the Commonwealth, Turkey has ignored all resolutions and pleas for justice in Cyprus and has continued to support the Turkish pseudo state which Turkey alone recognizes.
Justice for Cyprus means the removal of Turkish troops and Turkish colonists from Cyprus, the return of the 200,000 refugees, an accounting of the 2,000 missing Cypriots and their release from Turkish jails. It means a free, united Cyprus as stated in UN Resolution 37/253 which was adopted in 1983.
If we are to achieve justice in Cyprus, we must have a clear understanding of who the aggressors and the victims are. This is not a problem between Greek and Turkish Cypriots and it is not an insoluble problem as the Turkish Government would like to portray it. It is nothing but the occupation by an aggressor of a small island country with a limited defence.

Speech:
One of the major problems with indexing is that it feeds itself. It validates the inflation. There is a provision in this Bill which reduced indexation with respect to tax allowances and the tax rate by expecting people to absorb the first 3 per cent of any inflation that takes place. We expect
Income Tax Act, 1986
citizens to absorb some of the costs of inflation because, unless we do so, inflation protection measures continue to feed the inflation that we want to reduce.
It is important for the House to realize that the Government cannot continue to index everything and expect to balance the Budget. One of the major causes of the serious shortage of revenue as against expenditures which exists in our budgetary process has been the result of the indexation that has been extended to all of our social programs and our tax system. Before indexation was brought in on a broad scale to cover pensions, and every other form of benefit, allowance, or charge of the Government, generally speaking Governments were very close to balancing their budgets. Since then our deficit has grown year after year, and often more in good years than in bad years.
Speaking in round figures, for every dollar we spend we only bring in 65 cents in taxes. The other 35 cents must either be borrowed, printed, or somehow taken away from pension reserves. That policy cannot go on. However, that is the social policy advocated by the Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith). His social policy is that it is all right to borrow, and that it is all right to pledge the future of your children, that of their children, and that of their children's children, as long as we have it today.
That is not our policy. Our policy is to attack the root of inflation by refusing to validate it. Our policy is to collect more revenue to reduce our shortfall. I am sorry that means more taxes in some senses. That is the purpose of this section and that is why it is in the Bill. I do not think anyone in the House really wants to pay more taxes. No one wants to pay more taxes, but we as Canadians, as a responsible Party, and a responsible Government, tell ourselves that we have to pay our way. In that sense, the amendment is irresponsible because it says: "Sir, I want more cake, I want more, more, more, and I don't want to pay for it". I am surprised that the Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) brought that position to the House. I would understand it from his Party, but not from him.
Inflation feeds on itself. Indexation validates inflation. It may be necessary for the Government to take one step further and abolish all forms of indexing, because we cannot forever increase payments to people and reduce taxes to people because the cost of living continues to go up. When we do that the cost of living is just passed on and the next year's cost of living goes up. We saw how that worked when we had a provision whereby liquor and tobacco taxes were indexed to the cost of living. We imposed taxes, the price of the articles went up, and that justified a further increase in taxes. Therefore, we imposed more taxes, the price of the article went up, and that justified further increases in taxes.
Here it works exactly the opposite. When the price goes up, we reduce the tax. We have less money to pay Government expenditures, but because we are also going to index benefits, as the price of things go up we increase benefits. Again, our deficit is smaller, our tax revenue goes down, and our expenditures go up. Of course we have this massive, built-in, perma-

nent deficit. It is time the House got down to brass tacks and got rid of that deficit. We cannot get rid of it unless we are prepared to pay the cost, part of which is this clause which must remain in the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, as we enter into the last two days of debate on Bill C-70, the Bill to deindex the family allowance and the amendments thereto, I believe it is incumbent upon us as Members of Parliament to review the process whereby we arrive at this stage of the Bill today.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, as will the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), that, in essence, the commencement of this debate began in November of 1984, some two months after the Conservative Government assumed office. The Government promised in the Economic Statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that Canadians from all walks of life would have the opportunity to enter into a debate and a review of family benefits, and the Government talked as well about the need for a review of elderly benefits.
From mid-November, 1984 to the end of January, 1985, there was considerable debate on the floor of the House of Commons about the actual intentions of the Government with respect to the two papers which would have been tabled with the Economic Statement of November, 1984. I recall very well some of the promises made at that time not only by the Minister of National Health and Welfare but by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance. They gave us the reasons and the rationale for the kind of debate they wanted to have concerning both those papers. I can recall very well the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicating that the purpose of the review was simply to ensure that the benefits would flow to those targeted groups in our
January 16, 1986

society who need more help than others and that under no circumstances would any savings as a result of the review of child benefits be targeted for deficit reduction. That was one promise made by the Government.
In addition, I recall at the beginning of this debate that the Prime Minister, in his own words, questioned the rationale behind a bank president receiving family allowance benefits. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, as a result of the heated debate on the floor of the House of Commons and the Opposition's defence of the universality of those two programs, the Government retreated. That led to the tabling of the position paper of the Government, the white paper on family benefits, by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in January of 1985. The whole matter was then referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. We in turn, for several months, had many, many groups appear before the committee to give us some suggestions as to how better to structure family benefits programs, and all three political Parties agreed with the necessity of better targeting the resources to those in our society who needed help the most. I can recall that we did have an all-Party agreement when we returned to the House of Commons from committee for the report stage with a set of suggestions which would improve the delivery of the family benefits system. I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare will recall that we indicated to him that we favoured the removal of the child exemptions and the improvement of the child tax credit. In addition, we also recommended that the cross-over point, the point at which the child tax credit value begins to diminish, should be increased because we felt that under the proposal made by the Government at the time, a $23,00 a year family income was far too low a level for the cross-over to occur. We recommended it should be higher than $23,000. We also suggested that the StatsCan definition of middle income families should be the cross-over point at which the Government should look at improving the system for family benefits.
I feel that, realistically, had the Government taken the advice of the committee, and had the improvements to the family benefit packages which were announced on May 23 been taken into account, we could have had an improvement in the delivery of family benefits which would have resulted in better targeting to those in our society who need more help.
Unfortunately, the Government chose to ignore the recommendations of the standing committee, and if one takes a look at the minute details which are inherent in Bill C-70, one can see that not only did the Government reject the majority of the advice given by that committee but it in effect, in my view, proceeded in a retroactive way in creating a family benefit system for this country which is going to worsen the lot of those in our society who need help the most, namely the lower-income families.
As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, we indicated in debates previous to this part of third reading, that we have a great deal of concern about the plans to deindex the child tax credit beginning in the year 1989 and beyond. Here we have a Government that could have improved the situation had it left

Mr. Speaker, 1 recognize the concerns of the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Jepson) with respect to the adequacy of the Young Offenders Act to deal with young offenders. The Young Offenders Act has significantly altered the orientation of Canada's juvenile justice system. The old Juvenile Delinquents Act was based on a philosophy that emphasized the need to treat delinquents as children in need of care and assistance rather than as criminals. The specific provisions of that legislation reflected this principle in many ways that were increasingly inconsistent with contemporary values and laws.
For example, the Juvenile Delinquents Act intended that juvenile court proceedings be private and closed to the public and that information about those proceedings be treated as confidential. Similarly, because delinquents were not to be treated as criminals, police were generally not permitted to take fingerprints, and it was not clear whether juvenile records

January 16, 1986
Adjournment Debate
could be used in adult court when a young person continued his criminal behaviour into adulthood.
The emphasis of the old Act on the needs of the offender was particularly evident in its dispositional or sentencing provisions. When the juvenile court found that sanctions such as probation were not sufficient to deal with an individual, the Act provided for the case to be tranferred to the care of child welfare authorities, rather than ordering a specific sentence which would be served under the jurisdiction of the criminal justice system.
By way of contrast, the Young Offenders Act has clearly acknowledged that young people are responsible for their illegal behaviour and that society has a fundamental right to protection. The new legislation has not abandoned the principle that young people have special needs that demand the attention of the juvenile justice system and society as a whole, but it places this issue in perspective. The principle that the protection of society must be a primary concern is reflected in the legislation.
For example, the Act authorizes police to take fingerprints, just as they do when investigating adult offenders, as was mentioned by the Hon. Member. Criminal records are now clearly available to the criminal justice system, including the adult court, unless they are subject to destruction following a specified period of crime-free behaviour by the young person. Under the new legislation young offenders are subject to incarceration in correctional facilities and remain under the jurisdiction of the youth court throughout their sentences. As a result, a young person must serve the entire sentence in custody unless the youth court authorizes early release.
For the most serious of cases, the act permits a youth court to transfer a serious charge to adult court. Where such a transfer is ordered, the youth will be subject to all the penalties that an adult would face, up to and including life imprisonment.
It is fully appreciated that in implementing such important changes in the orientation of juvenille justice, difficulties will be encountered and some of these require legislative change. The Solicitor General has held consultations in Vancouver, Toronto, Regina, Montreal, and Moncton to discuss the Act with representatives of police departments, youth courts, private sector agencies dealing with young offenders, and other groups involved in youth justice in Canada, including his counterparts in the provinces and territories.
In summary, 1 would like to assure the Hon. Member that the Minister is well apprised of the concerns with the Young Offenders Act and is prepared to respond fairly and effectively to those areas which clearly require change.

Many very good points have been made about family allowances in this debate. However, for me there are two crucial aspects to the history of family allowance in Canada. First, when family allowances came into being, our society recognized by state action the value of children by earmarking a very specific sum of money to be directed to children in society. That was an important action. Normally, in most of our transactions, a good part of which is totally justified in a market economy, people have the freedom to choose how they dispose of their incomes. That is part of what freedom is all about. However, my Party has long held the view that the allocation of financial resources in society ought never to be exclusively determined by market considerations.
Historically, the fundamental reason we came into being was that we favoured the view that society itself, through its elected men and women, ought to interfere with the marketplace constructively, positively and without embarrassment to
Family Allowances Act, 1973
decide that there are certain collective goals for the community as a whole that ought to be met by spending income. When we decided many years ago on family allowances, we were saying as a society that children and families are important and that the state is earmarking a particular sum of money to go to the children of our society. That is important and has become part of our social history.
The second important aspect of family allowances is something which, though not intended as such, was immediately perceived and has remained, and that is, what it has meant for many women in Canadian society. The point that has now been recognized by members of all Parties but is not made today is that the only cheques many women in Canadian society receive in their own names are the family allowance cheques, and that is a very important consideration. I am sure Members on all sides of the House have run into women in rural Canada, urban Canada, the Atlantic provinces, the West, downtown Toronto and downtown Montreal who have said that the family allowance cheques, though perhaps they are not an awful lot in dollar value except for low-income families, are important to them because the cheques come in their names. These two points are very important. I would suggest that a Government sensitive to these elements of social justice in our past would not be changing them now for the future.
Some 40 years ago family allowances were introduced. I would argue that they have an important place in the shared set of social values which most Canadians support. Without going into all the details of the history from that point in time onward, I do wish to mention a few crucial points.

Double Taxation
More and more now Canadians are going abroad and involving themselves in entrepreneurial initiatives and doing business in other countries. Of course, until these tax treaties are arranged, it means that people are often taxed twice, once in the country in which they are doing business, and again in the country of their citizenship. In a sense, Bill S-6 ensures that income earned will only be taxed once. I suppose that as far as the Government is concerned that is not a major item, but it is a signal that the Government now sends out to Canadian investors and business people that doing business in India, the USSR, and Guyana will now be made easier. The matter of taxation of one's personal affairs will not be jeopardized by being involved in business or work of one kind or another in these three countries.
Having had the opportunity in the last number of months to travel to both India and the Soviet Union on Government matters, it seems to me that this is a very timely and important Bill. The opportunities for enhanced trade, to do business, and to make deals in the U.S.S.R. and India particularly, are quite limitless. The country of India is booming industrially. It needs a great deal. It can use much of the technology that has been developed to a high level in Canada, whether in telecommunications, transportation, or the construction of hydro electric works. There is an opportunity, not only for Canadians to involve themselves in doing business in these countries, but also for Canada to play a role, particularly in countries like Guyana and India, in terms of assisting their development toward self-reliance and self-determination in economic terms.
I am very impressed with the advances that the poor country of India has made in terms of developing its industrial and communication infrastructure. I was quite amazed that one can actually send a letter from Bombay to Calcutta in one day. This is a country of nearly 800 million people and 800,000 villages. Yet, its mail system is very sophisticated relative to ours. The development of transportation and hydro electric systems is escalating, to a large extent, because of Canadian technology and assistance from both the private and the public sectors.

The average world military expenditure for each soldier is over 50 times that of average public spending on education for every school-aged child. He says there are tens of thousands of teachers, religious leaders, lawyers, scientists, students and parents committed to devoting their energies to a wide range of activities, both political and educational in nature.

Mr. Speaker, the derailment of a CP Rail train yesterday near Raith, not far from Thunder Bay, focuses the problems we face in ensuring safe train movement. The derailment, which fortunately occurred in a sparsely-populated area, was the result of a roller bearing burn out. This happened 45 kilometres past one hot box detector and 10 kilometres short of the next one. The technological problem is that burn outs occur more rapidly with roller bearings than with steel axles in brass seats. This means roller bearings fail with very little warning. One of the recommendations of the Grange Inquiry into the Mississauga derailment was that roller bearings should be installed on all tank cars. That recommendation is now in question.

I call upon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) to institute a thorough investigation of these technological challenges. Derailment of trains, especially in the winter-time, appear to be inevitable in our rail transportation system. Let us be sure that on the trains and elsewhere we have all the means to deal with them as safely as possible.

With respect to the exact timing, Your Honour will know that letters and copies indicating the intention were delivered to your office in advance of personal delivery, which took place at or about 4.30 p.m. in the aftternoon. Prior to that members of my staff were in touch by telephone with the Hon. House Leader for the Opposition, as he points out. Opposition Parties were notified of our intention to designate those two days as allotted days.
Second, in spite of the fact that steps were taken by me advising all appropriate persons, and in spite of the fact that opposition Parties walked out of the House, it is clear that, in any event, the Official Opposition filed a motion for debate on this day. Third, may I remind Your Honour of the fact that, pursuant to Standing Order 63(1), we have a continuing order for the consideration of the business of supply which enables Opposition Parties to file motions for consideration at any time prior to the time when that item of business is before the House. February 3, 1986

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, during the submissions of the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) he said: "Nothing should be done to bring the administration of justice into disrepute". If there is anything that would bring the administration of justice into disrepute, it is the presumption of guilt before a fair hearing by a particular tribunal.
I cannot help but point out the hypocrisy in the position of the Solicitor General. When he was the Minister of National Revenue, he put together what was known as the Declaration of Taxpayer Rights. I am sure you recall when he put that out, Mr. Speaker. He said that henceforth the taxpayers of Canada would have certain rights and he proceeded to point out what those rights are.
One of those rights, and this is a document put out by the Solicitor General when he was the Minister of National Revenue, was the presumption of honesty. He said: "You are entitled to be presumed honest unless there is evidence to the contrary". He went on to say that "you are entitled to every benefit allowed by the law".
One could ask the Solicitor General why taxpayers should be allowed every benefit allowed by the law yet members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police not be entitled to every benefit allowed by the law? The law of Canada is the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms which states at Clause 1 \(d) that a resident of Canada:
to be presumed innocent until proven guilty according to law in a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal.
The Solicitor General says nothing should be done to bring the administration of Justice into disrepute. His position of not allowing members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to be suspended with full pay and benefits brings the administration of justice into disrepute because it presumes that an officer is guilty of some offence. Why else would you suspend an officer without pay? One could conclude that by suspending

February 5, 1986
RCMP Act
an officer without full pay and benefits that the particular officer is guilty of some offence.
The Solicitor General says that in certain cases the infraction might be so serious that it demands the officer be suspended without pay. The Solicitor General then cited the example of a bank robbery.
A person is presumed and assumed innocent, regardless of the evidence prior to a trial. Yet the Solicitor General is suggesting that in the case of someone charged with bank robbery he or she should be suspended without full pay and benefits. Is the Solicitor General not saying that the commissioner, in this particular case, has the authority to condemn an officer or a member of the Force who is still innovent according to the law of Canada? It is a basic and fundamental principle of our justice system that one is presumed innocent until proven guilty. I cannot understand why the Solicitor General is so adamant in his position that he wants to suspend members of the Force without pay and benefits.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) and other Hon. Members have indicated why an individual should not be suspended without full pay and benefits. We in the Official Opposition believe-and I am sure the NDP would agree- that all members who are in the midst of an investigation should be suspended with full pay and benefits or assigned to other duties. Otherwise, the person is being convicted before he or she is given a fair hearing, before the person's final guilt is determined. It is a preliminary finding of guilt if the person is suspended. It is not only contrary to the basis of the justice system in Canada, but on humanitarian and compassionate grounds, and on those grounds alone, one could argue that a member of the Force should not be suspended without full pay and benefits and that indeed one should be suspended with full pay and benefits.
Can we imagine the hardship involved for a member of the Force who is suspended without full pay and is subjected to a long hearing or investigation? Let us say that it takes from six months to a year before the RCMP conducts its own investigation into a particular allegation. What is the particular member who is presumed innocent supposed to do? He or she is denied full pay and benefits. Presumably some of the benefits are for the member's family, so the family suffers as a result. Is he or she to go on welfare? Is he or she to go on unemployment insurance? We can see how serious the matter is, if the commissioner is allowed to suspend an individual without full pay and benefits.
After the final determination of the particular allegation, if the person is found to have contravened the code of conduct or the Criminal Code of Canada, after he or she has been found guilty, we all agree that then and only then should the commissioner be allowed to suspend the person without pay. Otherwise it would create considerable harship.
In closing, I reiterate my very serious concerns about the hypocrisy of the position taken by the Solicitor General. When he was Minister of National Revenue he had what is known as
the "Declaration of Taxpayer Rights". It was a high-faluting document. He had it framed. It went across the country. He was very proud of it. He was also proud of the fact that there was a presumption of honesty and that every taxpayer was entitled to every benefit allowed by the law. What has changed his mind since he was made the Solicitor General of Canada? Why should RCMP officers and members not be afforded the same rights as any other Canadian is afforded? Those rights include the right to be presumed innocent until proven guilty. I, for one, cannot understand that blatant and obvious hypocrisy.

Speech:
Rather than continually formulating amendments which will be voted down without any real consideration by this large Conservative majority, I have better ways to spend my time. It is too bad that those amendments were defeated.
On this particular amendment, there was wide-spread and deep support among the members of the Force. They made that clear before the committee. It was something which was also recommended by the Marin Commission, which spent a good deal of time consulting and studying the issue, not only in Canada with other police forces but outside the country as well.
The other matter the Bill does not deal with, and which I think is unfortunate, is leaving the final decision on public complaints with the Commissioner rather than with an independent authority. That is contrary to all the principles of justice and equity. If one is responsible for the administration of a body, in this case the RCMP, then it is not proper that that person should be the final judge on accusations or complaints made by the public against members of the Force while administering the Force at the same time. That person then becomes both judge and administrator. To me that is not proper. It is unfortunate that the Government has not seen fit to accept an amendment along these lines.
I am pleased to recall that during my term as Solicitor General certain improvements were made to the personnel policy with respect to the RCMP. At that time we brought in,
RCMP Act
for the first time, overtime pay for members of the Force, changes with respect to the marriage rules and the admittance of women into the Force, and the division representative system was set up. The division representative system was certainly a movement in the right direction. According to some members of the Force it is working well.
However, there is still a difficulty in that the RCMP in many of our large cities must work side-by-side with other police forces on joint efforts. The members of those other police forces have the right to collective bargaining. Collective bargaining has been tried in our police forces in the country for several years. It has not been abused.
At the time of the introduction of the division representative system there was not that much experience with collective bargaining. That was in the mid 1970s. I want to make it clear that I am talking about the right to collective bargaining and not the right to strike. The Association of 17 Divisions has not asked for the right to strike. The other police forces in Canada have the right to collective bargaining and they do not have the right to strike. So we are not debating the right to strike issue. However, after this number of years, having seen what has taken place with other police forces in the country, and in light of the fact that the RCMP must work shoulder-to-shoul-der in many cases on drug and organized crime matters with provincial and municipal police forces which have the right to collective bargaining, I believe the time has come for the RCMP to have the right to collective bargaining.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby is right when he says that the Liberal Party did not always take that position. As 1 have said, we have observed what has happened over the years. By the way, we in the Liberal Party are much more broadly based than those in the NDP. We have a much wider range of opinions. We have people in our Party who always believed in the right to collective bargaining and others who did not.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make a few comments about these amendments which have been so long in gestation that there must be people who have retired and died since they were originally proposed back in the 1960s. It is scandalous that so many pension plans seem to be designed to benefit not the employee but only the employer. They give the illusion of protection but it is not followed through. The rules for vesting are so inappropriate because they require that an employee attain the age of 45 and have more than 10 years of service before benefits can be vested. That is being changed in this Bill and it is a welcome change. However, it has taken a heck of a long time to get to that point. I believe the reason for that is that the employers and the pension industry have not wanted those changes to be made. I want to go on record as condemning their record and their failure to understand the necessity of providing income security for that large number of people who work for employers where there are pension plans regulated under federal or provincial legislation.
When I was in the Ontario Legislature the question of pension reform came up frequently. We had a royal commission. It was studied by a legislative committee. Vast amounts of studies and research were produced. However, what we could not get around was the lack of political will by the Conservative Government of Ontario and the then Liberal Government of Canada to make the necessary moves. The only place where reform really came forward was in the Province of Manitoba under an NDP Government. That province decided, regardless of the failure of other provinces and the federal Government to move, that they would make the necessary and desirable reforms in order to ensure that employees who contributed to pension plans had a good chance of actually benefiting from them.
We finally have some changes. They are watered down and inadequate. In particular, they are objectionable because they only apply after 1987. The NDP is supporting this Bill. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, supposing, in my opinion correctly, that Canadians had the right to know how much they were paying their public employees, prior to 1919 the Government of Canada published the Civil Service List annually. For example, the 1916 Civil Service List reveals that Mr. Edmund Newcombe, Deputy Minister of Justice, was paid an annual salary of $10,000, and that Mr. David Gillespie, bridgekeeper on the Cornwall Canal, was paid a wage of $2 a day. It is not to be supposed, Sir, that either Mr. Newcombe or Mr. Gillespie suffered from having their emoluments made public, any more than MPs and Senators do today.
For some unknown reason the Government of the present time refuses to make known specific salaries and benefits paid to its employees. This has especially been the case with senior employees of Crown corporations. At best, a rather meaningless salary range will be given.
Taxpayers are naturally suspicious of the motives of a Government which hides, for no apparent good reason, the use of their money behind a screen of secrecy. Therefore, let us follow the eminent good sense of our forebears and let this information be known.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the accumulated past debt symbolizes a kind of mismanagement which still shakes confidence in Canada. The debt is growing faster than our economy. Our debt, as a percentage of GNP, is one of the highest in the industrialized world. Recent downward pressure on the dollar and rising interest rates, while due in part to speculation, also reflect concern about the deficit and our resolve to do something about it.
Clearly, we must renew and strengthen our determination to deal with the deficit. The course charted in the November, 1984, economic statement and the May, 1985, Budget is correct. Most individual Canadians feel that they are now taxed to the limit. I think they are right.
I, therefore, suggest that the attack on the deficit should concentrate on three broad fronts; first, by reducing Government involvement and expenditure through the elimination of waste and the discarding of programs which are non-essential; second, by re-examining some social programs to direct payments only to those who are genuinely in need; and, third, by eliminating a number of corporate and individual preferences such as grants, exemptions, subsidies, investment tax credits, excessive capital cost allowances and tax deferrals. Deficit reduction will lead to renewed confidence, more growth, even more jobs, and greater prosperity for all Canadians.

Just a few words, Mr. Speaker. I say in all honesty that I think one of the primary things that should take place in a legislature under the British parliamentary system in the 1980s is certainly to have a full and complete debate on the proposition of having a permanent Speaker. Perhaps that is one of the two important subjects that should be dealt with in a debate in this Chamber such as this.
The other thing that should be dealt with is a subject that some Members do not want to deal with, and it is this. I was listening to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) the other day when he said that he would like to restore the power to Members of Parliament in this Chamber. He said that he would like to bring this House of Commons into the 20th century in the great British tradition. The other part of the question that has to be dealt with, if that is what the Prime Minister wants to do, is, first and foremost, that Members of Parliament will have to allow an impartial body exterior to this Chamber to have the power to make changes in the procedures of this House.
Members here in this House and members of the committee would say, "Well, that's a terrible thing to suggest". Not so, Mr. Speaker. If you were going to follow the British tradition or the traditions of any legislature under the British parliamentary system you would, first and foremost, have to accept that as being necessary for complete change, because that is exactly what the other legislatures-if I can refer to them generally-have done. They are Parliaments, but they are more than Parliaments-from the French word to speak- because they do more than that, they legislate. That is their primary function. How is that accomplished, Mr. Speaker? It was accomplished, first of all, by that body of Parliamentarians saying, "If we only allow ourselves to be restricted by our own suggestions, then we will never change and we will never get to the point where this Parliament become a legislative body". When the Prime Minister said, "Well, now, we would

like to get back to what the British parliamentary system was in this country", what he would have to be suggesting, in order to do that, to do what the British and the Australians have done, is to do what any legislature has done, and that is, to have an outside body recommend and implement rule changes in this legislature.
The other aspect is the question of a permanent Speaker. I think that all Members will agree that we have been particularly fortunate in this country over the last 10, 12, or 15 years. 1 believe that at any moment in time during that period either political Party could have instituted the position of permanent Speaker and there would not have been objections from the other side of the Chamber. Women in particular will be the victims of the Government's policies. There have been no directives coming from the political level of Government to ensure that the proportions laid off do not contain a disproportionate number of women. The evidence from Fisheries and other Departments is that a higher proportion of women are being cut back. I call upon the President of the Treasury Board to reverse that particular policy and announce it today.
Vital services are already being cut because of the $150 million cuts in the Public Service which have already been announced. The Government is cutting the Health and Welfare library. A valuable and irreplaceable national resource will be closed. Translation services, which are essential to Government in a bilingual country, are being cut back. Customs officers who, among other things, protect the country from the influx of drugs and pornography from abroad are being cut back. Canada Employment offices which help unemployed Canadians are being cut back in terms of the services which they can provide. Now the Government is taking a further step; we are told that in addition $500 million in non-statutory areas or almost four times as much will be cut.

February 27, 1986
Statements by Ministers
If the Government wanted the co-operation of public employees in making these cuts, it had ample room-and it has been demonstrated that it had ample room-to provide the job security protection which they sought and gain that cooperation. The 700 people which the President of the Treasury Board says will be cut back represent three-tenths of one per cent of the Public Service. If the pay agreement with the unions had been cut back by three-tenths of one per cent-and I am sure they would have accepted that-the money could have been found to save those 700 people from being thrust into a difficult job market. This does not only affect Ottawa, it affects the whole country. If the Government can find $500 million in the cuts announced in the Budget yesterday, it could have found the necessary sums to have kept those 700 jobs, allowing any changes in the Public Service to have taken place by attribution, not by the cuts which are now taking place.
The Government wanted to demonstrate to bankers that it could fire, that it could be tough, that it could be rough, just like back in the 1890s on the 1920s. That is what it wanted to do.

Especially as a result of the Budget. It has simply added to the same process; more and more on the backs of middle-income earners and less and less on the backs of the corporate sector.
As we all know average Canadians will be faced with a 3 per cent increase in their taxes as well as an increase in sales tax. What about upper-income earners? They receive a reduced tax as a result of the Budget. Their tax rate goes down. The situation is that upper-income earners and the corporate sector will have reduced tax rates as a result of the Budget and ordinary Canadian taxpayers will experience increases in their tax rates and in the sales tax.
People are asking about the real impact of this, how it can be measured and what it really means. It does not take much analysis to break it down in terms of what this Government has meant to Canadian families. If we look at the November 8, 1985 statement and tally up the costs as a result of it on the average Canadian family-and I am using for this example an average Canadian family of four with an income of $35,000 per year-we find that it resulted in $452 in increased costs.
If we look at the May 23, 1985 Budget, we find that the increased costs to that same family as a result of the modification to indexation, the cut in family allowance payments, the increased taxes on cigarettes, alcohol and gasoline and the sales tax increase, amounted to $512.50. Then we have the Budget of February 26, yesterday. When we add up the costs as a result of it the very conservative total, if I may use that term, comes to $340. If we add up the totals as a result of that economic statement and those Budgets, we find that the increase from the federal Government alone amounts to $1,304.50 for an average Canadian family of four. It is the largest tax grab in modern history, in recent times.
We have never seen anything like this before, when a Government has gone in and ripped out more than $1,000 from Canadian families in just 14 months. This means that for every family in Canada-whether it be in Port Alberni, Red Deer, Thunder Bay, Chicoutimi, Moncton or St. Catharines, it does not matter where-in excess of $1,000 or $1,300 will not be circulating in those communities time and time again during the year to support the local economies. It has been
dragged out of those communities and down to Ottawa to be used for some highly questionable purposes.
What are those purposes? Let us look at how the tax system is used. We asked for a major overhaul of the tax system because we were convinced that the hidden spending which takes place through the shelters, loopholes and various tax expenditure programs comes to billions and billions of dollars each year, and they are never evaluated. We asked the Government to look at these tax expenditure programs and to evaluate them to see whether or not we are getting good value for the money. If we have a program which is designed to encourage the construction of low-income rental housing, is it doing that? Of course when we look at the program it never does that. Is the use of the tax system to encourage mining exploration the most effective way of accomplishing that? We have to ask these questions. Was there one mention of tax reform, tax overhaul or evaluating the value of those tax dollars in the Budget? Not a word, not a word.
Let us look at the incredible amount of money involved in the tax system. One of the favourite areas people mention is the amount of taxes known as deferred corporate taxes. It now approaches nearly $30 billion annually. Numbers of corporations do not pay; they simply defer their taxes year after year. Mr. Speaker, when you and I do not pay any income tax or make a mistake on our income tax return and owe money to the Government, we pay interest on it whether it is two weeks or two months.

Mr. Speaker, my Parliamentary Secretary makes a very valid observation with respect to the juxtaposition of regulatory reform in connection with the total fiscal and economic policy of this Government. A task force dealt with regulatory reform and looked at the wide ranging implications of regulations for Canada. It was pointed out by way of example-and this was the most conservative assertion possible on the basis of advice we received from experts in the field-that regulations impact on Canadians to the extent of some $30 billion. Consider that in the regulatory process there are some 35,000 public servants involved directly and, I suppose, indirectly. This means that a very large part of Government is involved in law-making behind the scenes. This has a very serious and wide-ranging effect on the daily lives of Canadians. Regulations cover food inspection, hazardous products, transportation, shipping and fisheries, to name a few, not to mention agriculture which is a matter of substantial importance to me, being from the Province of Saskatchewan. This gives you an idea of the wide range of activities affected by regulations which are not made on the floor of the House of Commons. They are created behind the scenes and promulgated in a conveyer belt process, as I said, by Cabinet.
What we are doing now is trying to bring some light to the process. It is absolutely essential, for example, that we enter into a process where all new regulations are measured against their social cost and cost efficiency so that a judgment can be made by the people involved in the political life of our country, including Members of Parliament, as to their validity.
I say this in all seriousness to the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan). He has had some experience with regulations, as have I, in sitting for many years on that committee. If the people of Canada had an opportunity to look at this, they would be astounded and amazed just how much law and constraint on their activities is effected outside of this Chamber. There is a phenomenal amount of regulation of people taking place.
For example, the committee has been doing excellent work in examining whether or not officials are arbitrary; whether or not our freedoms are negatively affected by regulations; whether or not principles of natural justice are observed in the drawing up of regulations. These laws, and that is what they are, are drawn up in the bureaucracy without the same sort of scrutiny that laws in the statute books receive on the floor of this House. There are certainly no television cameras watching and no public discussion. It is done by people who have a responsibility but also a kind of self-interest with respect to the nature and form of regulations. In my view, the Parliamentary Secretary has highlighted the significance of this problem and the necessity for the Government to enter into a new regime of measuring what is being done regarding the economic welfare of Canadians.
I do not want to take any more time but I do want to reiterate that under this new regime Canadians are going to become, so far as the federal level is concerned, world leaders in regulatory reform. This is a very, very progressive initiative we are taking. I am very proud to be associated with it because I know the long history of this issue. I say this is a non-partisan sense. There has been a desire by all Parties to come to grips with the growing volume of regulation and make sure there is some rationale to the regulations which affect the daily lives of our fellow citizens so very much.

Mr. Speaker, today is Commonwealth Day and it gives me great pleasure to salute this remarkable institution. We are all familiar with the spirit of friendship and tolerance which so distinguishes this association of 49 states comprising fully one-quarter of the world's population. Its specific achievements are many, and we quite naturally think of the Commonwealth as an association where peoples from around the world reach across the great divides of religion, race, and economic and political philosphies to establish a commonality of purpose which draws on our diversity and is nourished by it.
Canada needs the Commonwealth and Canadians, by temperament, are well suited to playing a leadership role there. A nation's foreign policy is grounded in the needs, interests, aspirations, and talents of its people. We in Canada are fortunate to have two official languages and many different cultural and ethnic traditions. We have, against great odds, built a country which is second to none in its respect for the rights of others and, most especially, for the right to a life of dignity regardless of race, religion, or creed.

It is no accident that the Commonwealth so accurately reflects these fundamental values of our country. We were present when the organization was established, and from the very outset, Canadians have been active and energetic participants. More than any other multilateral institution, the Commonwealth has been shaped by Canadian values and reflects the driving forces behind our foreign policy.
Mr. Speaker, this country abhors the system of apartheid. It was John Diefenbaker who spearheaded the movement to expel South Africa from the Commonwealth, a spectacular act that sharply focussed the attention of the world, more than ever before, on this shameful situation. Last year in Nassau, it was again the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) who decisively influenced the Commonwealth Agreement on South Africa.

Going into Nassau there were many who feared that the South Africa question could damage the meeting, could perhaps damage the Commonwealth itself, beyond all repair. We did not share this pessimism. We have confidence in our traditional foreign policy skills and the ways in which those skills have served Canada and the Commonwealth so well over the years.
In Nassau we set a timetable for the dismantling of apartheid and the initiation of reforms. We established a group of eminent persons to facilitate dialogue and work for powersharing arrangements that might avert a catastrophe in South Africa. That group is now in South Africa and Canada is ably represented by Archbishop Edward Scott in its deliberations.
The Commonwealth has been important to the pursuit of other Canadian foreign policy objectives: The transformation of Rhodesia to the new Zimbabwe, the growing acceptance of women as equal partners in economic and political life, and the efforts to move forward on north-south economic issues. In these and similar areas the Commonwealth has made significant contributions. Indeed, the success of the Commonwealth inspired much of the thinking which went into the hosting of the first ever Summit of Francophone Nations last month in Paris. We have great hopes that this francophone forum, too, will become an instrument for international understanding and human progress.

Canada's foreign policy is conducted through a complex series of bilateral and multilateral associations and institutions. To better understand this country and its position in the world, we should identify the means by which we pursue our national objectives in agreement with our allies and friends the world over. Our foreign policy is distinct because we have a unique network of international relations. Outside the Commonwealth, no other institution reflects so profoundly the way we feel about ourselves.

Canada has invited Commonwealth leaders to convene in Vancouver in 1987 for their next meeting. The invitation demonstrates our commitment to the Commonwealth, and the Vancouver meeting will demonstrate to Canadians the Commonwealth's attachment to and respect for Canada and the principles which guide this country in our activities around the world.

A deduction means nothing to most of the handicapped since about 1.8 per cent of the disabled earn incomes which place them in taxable brackets. Therefore, if the Government wished to do anything for the disabled, it would be something in the nature of a credit such as was provided to mothers looking after children at home. This was a credit introduced by the former Government which put money into the pockets of those most in need. That is not accomplished here. Nothing is done for those, if 1 can put it ironically, but the best-off among the handicapped, the ones who have to pay income tax.
This is a measure introduced by a Minister who bragged about being proud to help the very poor and that this was what his Government was all about. As I was looking at what was done for the handicapped, my eye fell on the chart at page 42 of The Fiscal Plan which shows that the cost to the Government of the measure which was introduced in its first full year of operation, that is 1986-87, is zero. Therefore I asked the Minister about it. I asked him how he could say that he was helping those handicapped who pay income tax, that very small percentage of handicapped who are able to earn an income which puts them in a tax bracket of zero. The answer he gave was that the effects of the change this year will not be felt until the next taxation year as the tax returns come in. I reject that answer because 1986-87 is the first fiscal year in which these tax changes come into effect. That is the year which begins at the end of April and includes the end of the 1986 taxation year of all individual taxpayers. Therefore, it includes the handicapped. If this benefit shows anything, it should show some cost to the Treasury as of the end of that taxation year, which is included in the Government's 1986-87 fiscal year.
This is why I wished to draw this matter to the attention of the House and of the country. 1 do so in order to show just how cheap the Government is. It does this in an attempt to disguise the heavy burden of this Bill and the former Budget on taxpayers, especially the poor and those toward the bottom end of the scale. The Government has thrown them little concessions which in this case amount to nothing and, in the case of the sales tax credit, very little. 1 wish to expose the Government for what it is doing, which is taking with one hand and taking with the other.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to announce that the Government has decided to produce a new Canadian one-dollar coin. As a consequence, 1 will be introducing amendments to the Currency Act at the earliest opportunity.
[ Translation]
As the Minister responsible for the Royal Canadian Mint, I have asked the Master of the Mint to strike a one-dollar coin that will be in circulation by January 1987.
Mr. Speaker, the concept of a one-dollar coin is not new. The Members of this House will recall that the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates held hearings on the subject last year and published a report recommending that a coin of this denomination be issued.

The Mint will initially produce 300 million one-dollar coins. Each coin will be made of an aureate bronze plated on pure nickel. This will mean a one-time requirement for five million pounds of nickel coin blanks, and an annual demand for half a million pounds. We believe this requirement will have a positive impact on jobs in the Canadian mining industry.
The coin will be struck at the Royal Canadian Mint in Winnipeg where all of Canada's circulating coinage is presently produced. The technology involved in this type of production run will continue to keep Canada in the forefront of the coinage production industry, resulting in enhanced opportunities for offshore orders.
The coin will be 11-sided, slightly larger and heavier than a quarter, and gold coloured. Because of its shape it will be easily distinguishable from other coins, thus greatly beneficial to the visually impaired.
I also wish to advise the House that the Canadian one-dollar bill will be phased out of circulation following the introduction of the new dollar coin. This measure alone will result in savings of over $175 million in currency production costs over the 20-year life span of a circulating coin, as the existing dollar note has to be replaced each year.
Several organizations have called for a circulating dollar coin for years. The Canadian Urban Transit Association, representing the public transit authorities from across Canada, looks forward to the tremendous cost savings once processing of paper money used for fares is no longer required. Other groups, including vending machine operators and the visually impaired, are also strong proponents of this coin.
In summary, the Government is proceeding in this direction because we believe everyone in Canada stands to benefit. The circulating dollar will be of great importance to the mining industry, result in a tremendous saving to the taxpayer, and make cash transactions easier and more efficient for all concerned.
